events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Hellberg Safety investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current hearing-protection offering.. Constraints: Limited to publicly available information; no internal company data.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning.; Must consider existing B2B relationships and current reach to individual buyers.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, construction, medical).; 2) Expand the existing hearing-protection line into adjacent consumer segments without differentiation (e.g., standard earplugs for general use).; 3) No expansion: continue focusing on existing B2B hearing and face protection markets.; 4) Change route to market or customer group (e.g., sell directly to consumers online, partner with retailers, target a new demographic).; 5) Redesign existing products for a new use case (e.g., add comfort features for extended wear)..

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory that enhances outdoor activities and personal safety. Who benefits: Consumers seeking comfort and style during outdoor recreation and work; Hellberg Safety gains premium pricing and brand equity.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers view hearing protection as a fashion item and a status symbol, they will purchase multiple pairs and be willing to pay a premium for comfort and design.. How value is captured: Hellberg can charge higher prices for differentiated designs, sell through specialty retailers or direct-to-consumer channels, and capture value through brand loyalty and repeat purchases.. Assumptions: Consumers associate hearing protection with outdoor lifestyle and personal safety.; There is a market segment willing to pay a premium for comfort and design.; Hellberg can design and market a differentiated product without compromising safety standards.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% more for a hearing protector marketed as a lifestyle accessory.; Purchase intent will be higher for a product marketed with visible design features compared to a standard earplug.; Repeat purchase rate will be higher for a differentiated product than for a generic earplug..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive hearing protection as a medical necessity for specific health risks (e.g., noise-induced hearing loss). Who benefits: Consumers with hearing sensitivity; Hellberg Safety gains market share in health-conscious segments and can market safety as a medical requirement.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers view hearing protection as a health safeguard, they will purchase it even without lifestyle appeal, and may seek out products that meet specific medical standards.. How value is captured: Hellberg can price products at premium levels justified by safety certification, sell through medical supply channels, and capture value through repeat purchases of certified products.. Assumptions: Consumers associate hearing protection with health protection and are willing to pay for certified safety.; There is a segment of consumers with hearing sensitivity who prioritize medical compliance over design.; Hellberg can obtain or enhance certification without compromising product performance.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers with hearing sensitivity will indicate willingness to pay at least 15% more for a hearing protector certified to medical standards.; Purchase intent will be higher for a product marketed with medical certification compared to a standard earplug.; Repeat purchase rate will be higher for certified products than for non-certified generic earplugs..

Test "Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Lifestyle vs Medical Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging conditions. Participants are recruited from a panel of consumers with prior exposure to hearing protection. They view a description of a hearing protector and are asked: “How much would you be willing to pay for this product?”. Sample: 400 participants (200 per condition) to achieve 15% margin of error and 5% precision for a 20% difference in willingness to pay.. Measure: Average willingness to pay (in euros) for the lifestyle proposition (e.g., fashion, outdoor lifestyle) versus the medical proposition (e.g., hearing sensitivity, EN 352 certification).. Predictions: T1: Lifestyle condition will show a higher average willingness to pay than medical condition.; T2: Medical condition will show a higher average willingness to pay than lifestyle condition.. Decision rule: If the average willingness to pay for the lifestyle condition exceeds the medical condition by at least 15% (e.g., 15% higher), conclude T1 is supported. If the opposite difference is at least 15%, conclude T2 is supported. If neither difference exceeds 15%, the evidence is insufficient to decide.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory for outdoor recreation and personal safety, rather than a medical necessity. Begin with a limited pilot test (e.g., a direct-to-consumer online campaign) to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent for a lifestyle‑focused product. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory rather than a workplace requirement. Who benefits: Consumers seeking comfort, style, and convenience in hearing protection; Hellberg Safety gains premium pricing and brand extension.. Why behaviour changes: When hearing protection is framed as a fashion item or lifestyle accessory, consumers are more willing to purchase multiple pairs and pay a premium for design and comfort.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value through premium pricing, brand extension into fashion categories, and potential licensing of its design to lifestyle brands.. Assumptions: Consumers currently view hearing protection as a functional industrial item rather than a lifestyle accessory.; A differentiated proposition can effectively communicate the lifestyle aspect to consumers.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for design and comfort in hearing protection.. Predictions: In a test offering a lifestyle-branded hearing protection product, purchase intent and willingness to pay will be higher than for a standard industrial product.; Consumers will report higher satisfaction with the lifestyle product compared to a standard product.; Sales of the lifestyle product will be higher in markets where fashion and lifestyle are valued..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive hearing protection as a safety requirement for specific activities (e.g., construction, outdoor recreation) rather than a general lifestyle accessory. Who benefits: Safety-conscious consumers and employers who need reliable protection for work or recreational activities; Hellberg Safety gains market penetration in targeted segments.. Why behaviour changes: When hearing protection is positioned as essential for a specific activity, consumers are more likely to purchase it for that purpose, trusting the product's performance and compliance with safety standards.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value through targeted marketing, partnerships with safety providers, and premium pricing justified by the product's compliance and activity-specific performance.. Assumptions: Safety regulations and workplace standards require hearing protection for specific activities.; Consumers are aware of and trust safety-certified products for their intended use.; Hellberg's existing safety certification (EN 352) can be leveraged to demonstrate compliance for specific activities.. Predictions: In a test offering activity-specific hearing protection, purchase intent and sales will be higher than for a general lifestyle product.; Consumers will report higher confidence in the product's effectiveness for their specific activity.; Sales will be concentrated in regions or segments where the targeted activity is prevalent..

Test "Lifestyle vs Safety Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated product offers. Sample: 500 consumers recruited via a panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region (Europe). Randomly assigned to one of two message conditions.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and stated willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.. Predictions: T1: Lifestyle message will generate higher purchase intent and WTP than safety message.; T2: Safety message will generate higher purchase intent and WTP than lifestyle message.. Decision rule: If purchase intent for lifestyle message exceeds safety message by ≥15 percentage points and WTP for lifestyle exceeds safety by ≥€20, proceed with differentiated lifestyle proposition. If safety message exceeds lifestyle by ≥15 percentage points and WTP for safety exceeds lifestyle by ≥€20, pursue safety-focused proposition. If neither difference meets thresholds, maintain current model.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

T1: Private boat owners and outdoor enthusiasts will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition because they currently lack reliable, affordable emergency communication tools and would pay a premium for a device that reliably sends a distress signal via 406 MHz satellite, reducing their risk of being stranded or unreachable. Who benefits: Private boat owners and outdoor enthusiasts who face extended isolation at sea or in remote areas.. Why behaviour changes: They currently rely on traditional PLBs or cell phones, which may not reach a satellite or fail in emergencies, and they perceive the risk of being unreachable as high enough to justify a purchase.. How value is captured: ACR can capture value by selling a premium, differentiated product through retail and marine safety channels, leveraging its existing certification and brand credibility in emergency equipment.. Assumptions: There is a meaningful segment of private boat owners and outdoor enthusiasts willing to pay for a satellite distress beacon.; The 406 MHz technology is reliable and interoperable with existing emergency systems.; ACR can reach this segment through existing distribution channels or new retail partnerships.. Predictions: Surveyed boat owners will indicate high intent to purchase a satellite distress beacon if priced within $100-$150.; Pilot sales of a consumer product will generate at least 100 units in the first 12 weeks, indicating measurable demand..

T2: ACR's existing B2B customers (military and commercial marine users) will adopt a consumer proposition because they already trust ACR's emergency equipment and are willing to pay for a reliable, certified device that meets their safety requirements. Who benefits: ACR's current B2B customers who need reliable emergency communication for ships and aircraft.. Why behaviour changes: These customers already use ACR's products and are comfortable with certification and performance; they will extend that trust to a consumer product if it meets their safety standards.. How value is captured: ACR can capture value by leveraging its existing brand credibility and certification to sell a consumer product at a premium price, using the same distribution channels it uses for B2B sales.. Assumptions: ACR's B2B customers are willing to recommend or purchase a consumer product.; The consumer product will meet the same safety and performance standards expected by ACR's B2B customers.; ACR can reach B2B customers through existing channels and maintain brand trust.. Predictions: B2B customers will indicate high intent to purchase a consumer product if priced within $150-$200.; Pilot sales of a consumer product will generate at least 50 units from B2B customers in the first 12 weeks, indicating measurable demand from existing customers..

Test "Channel-Specific Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offers and price ranges, segmented by target audience (private boat owners vs. B2B customers). Participants view a product description and are asked to indicate purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum price they would pay. Recruitment is limited to U.S. and U.K. residents with boat ownership or commercial marine interest.. Sample: 300 respondents: 150 private boat owners/Outdoor enthusiasts (recruited via marine forums and outdoor groups) and 150 B2B decision-makers (recruited via trade associations and industry contacts).. Measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage of respondents saying "yes" when offered a $100-$150 price point) and maximum price willingness to pay.. Predictions: T1: Private boat owners will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than B2B customers across all price points.; T2: B2B customers will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than private boat owners across all price points.. Decision rule: If purchase intent for private boat owners exceeds that for B2B customers by at least 10 percentage points across all price points, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting private boat owners. If purchase intent for B2B customers exceeds that for private boat owners by at least 10 percentage points across all price points, pursue a B2B-focused consumer proposition. If neither segment meets the 10-point threshold, do not invest in a consumer proposition.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting private boat owners and outdoor enthusiasts, leveraging ACR's existing 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology. Begin with a limited pilot to test demand and price sensitivity before full-scale rollout. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence about a label printer reducing packing errors does not address consumer demand for a satellite distress beacon, so it does not affect T1. New claim: Private boat owners and outdoor enthusiasts will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition because they currently lack reliable, affordable emergency communication tools and would pay a premium for a device that reliably sends a distress signal via 406 MHz satellite, reducing their risk of being stranded or unreachable.. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting private boat owners and outdoor enthusiasts, leveraging ACR’s existing 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology. Begin with a limited pilot to test demand and price sensitivity before full-scale rollout. Target customer: Private boat owners and outdoor enthusiasts who face extended isolation at sea or in remote areas and currently lack reliable, affordable emergency communication tools.. Value proposition: A premium, differentiated consumer product that reliably sends a distress signal via 406 MHz satellite, reducing the risk of being stranded or unreachable, while leveraging ACR’s existing certification and brand credibility.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Channel-Specific Purchase Intent Test (300 respondents, 10‑week pilot) to measure purchase intent and price willingness for private boat owners versus B2B customers.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market and willingness to pay for a satellite distress beacon are uncertain. Evidence from 2002 shows ACR already had B2B customers and a product approved by the FCC, but no source shows consumer demand or price. Would change if: If the pilot shows purchase intent for private boat owners is at least 10 percentage points lower than for B2B customers across all price points, we would reconsider the consumer proposition and focus on B2B expansion.; If new evidence from 2002 shows a large, existing consumer market for marine safety devices or that ACR already had retail distribution, we would reassess the investment case.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

How value is captured: Hellberg can charge higher prices for differentiated designs, sell through specialty retailers or direct-to-consumer channels, and capture value through brand loyalty and repeat purchases.. Test "Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Lifestyle vs Medical Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with between‑subjects design. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two message frames: lifestyle (e.g., “Protect your hearing while enjoying the outdoors”) or medical (e.g., “Meeting legal safety standards for hearing protection”). They view a product description of a hearing protector meeting EN 352 standards and are asked: “How much would you pay for this product?”. Sample: 500 adults aged 18–65 in Europe, recruited via an online panel to ensure demographic diversity.. Measure: Average willingness-to-pay (WTP) in euros for the product described under each message frame.. Predictions: T1: Lifestyle frame will generate a WTP at least 20% higher than the medical frame.; T2: Medical frame will generate a WTP at least 15% higher than the lifestyle frame.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the lifestyle frame exceeds the average WTP for the medical frame by at least 20% (i.e., lifestyle ≥ × 1.2 – medical ≤ × 0.8), then T1 is supported and the recommendation is to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing lifestyle. If the medical frame exceeds the lifestyle frame by at least 15%, then T2 is supported and the recommendation is to develop a differentiated proposition emphasizing medical necessity. If neither difference meets the thresholds, the recommendation is to “. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Begin with a limited launch of a design‑focused product marketed through specialty retailers and direct‑to‑consumer channels, using the existing Hellberg brand and distribution network. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Next action: Run the proposed willingness‑to‑pay survey (or a smaller pilot) to test the impact of lifestyle messaging versus medical messaging, and use the results to decide whether to proceed with a full launch.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home users for a specific use case (e.g., weight management, fitness tracking).; 2) Expand the existing B2B offering by adding new features or marketing channels to clinics and health clubs without a consumer focus.; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B market (clinics and health clubs).; 4) License the technology to third‑party manufacturers to create consumer devices, capturing value through royalties rather than direct sales..

T1: Consumers will adopt home body-fat measurement if it is marketed as a health and wellness tool, because they already use bathroom scales and want to track body composition for diet and fitness. Who benefits: Individual health-conscious consumers seeking personal health insights.. Why behaviour changes: A shift from clinical use to personal health management makes the device appealing for daily tracking.. How value is captured: Tanita can sell premium-priced home devices directly to consumers through retail channels, capturing higher margins than B2B sales.. Assumptions: Consumers trust body-fat measurements as a health indicator.; Marketing can effectively communicate health benefits to home users.; Retail distribution is feasible within budget constraints.. Predictions: Willingness to pay for a home body-fat analyser will exceed the cost of a clinical version.; Purchase intent will be higher among consumers who cite health tracking as a primary reason.; Sales will be concentrated in regions with strong consumer health awareness..

T2: Consumers will adopt home body-fat measurement if it is marketed as a medical diagnostic tool for clinics and health clubs, because they trust professional validation and require accuracy for clinical decisions. Who benefits: Clinicians and health clubs seeking reliable body-fat data for patient care.. Why behaviour changes: Professional endorsement and clinical accuracy justify investment in a home device for professional use.. How value is captured: Tanita can sell high-accuracy clinical versions to clinics and health clubs, capturing value through volume sales and repeat purchases of calibration kits.. Assumptions: Clinical accuracy is a primary purchase driver for professional users.; Professional endorsement influences consumer perception of reliability.; Clinics are willing to invest in home devices for patient monitoring.. Predictions: Professional users will purchase home devices at higher prices than consumer versions.; Sales will be concentrated in regions with strong clinical presence.; Repeat purchases of calibration kits will be higher than single-use consumer devices..

T1 supports, from tanita-ht-household (independent_study): "In Japan, every household has a bathroom scale (health meter), and most nowadays keep track of your body composition.". Does not show: It does not show that consumers will purchase a home body-fat analyser or that they are willing to pay a premium for it..

T2 supports, from tanita-pm-radley (independent_study): "The Tanita TBF-310 foot-to-foot BIA body composition analyser with the manufacturer's prediction equations is not recommended for application to individual children who are overweight and obese". Does not show: It does not show that clinics and health clubs will purchase home devices for professional use, nor that they value clinical accuracy over consumer marketing..
Looked for evidence against T1: "consumer body fat scale market demand 1993"; found tanita-dic-origin, tanita-en-share, tanita-ht-household.

Test "Consumer vs Professional Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from health-conscious consumers (n=200) and clinical professionals (n=200). Each group views a product description of a home body-fat analyser. Consumer group sees health and wellness messaging; professional group sees clinical accuracy and professional endorsement. Both groups are offered a pre-order at a fixed price (proposed €199).. Sample: 200 consumers (health-conscious, self-reported interest in body composition tracking) and 200 professionals (clinicians, health club staff) from the US and Japan.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: pre-ordered) and stated willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.. Predictions: T1: Consumer group will show higher purchase intent and WTP than professional group.; T2: Professional group will show higher purchase intent and WTP than consumer group.. Decision rule: If consumer purchase intent exceeds professional purchase intent by at least 10 percentage points (e.g., 60% vs 50%), proceed to develop a consumer proposition. If professional purchase intent exceeds consumer purchase intent by at least 10 percentage points, pursue a B2B expansion. If both groups show similar intent, conduct further market research.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home body-fat measurement, targeting health-conscious individuals. Begin with a limited pilot to test demand and willingness to pay before full-scale production. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse label printing and does not address consumer demand, willingness to pay, or professional use of a home body-fat analyser. Therefore it provides no support or contradiction to T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home body-fat measurement, targeting health-conscious individuals. Begin with a limited pilot to test demand and willingness to pay before full-scale production. Target customer: Health-conscious consumers in Japan and the US who already use bathroom scales and want to track body composition for diet and fitness.. Value proposition: A premium-priced home body-fat analyser marketed as a personal health tool, leveraging Tanita’s established brand and clinical accuracy to provide actionable insights for daily tracking.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer vs Professional Messaging Test (or a smaller pilot) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay. If the consumer group shows a ≥ 10 percentage‑point advantage, proceed to develop the consumer product; if not,. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market and willingness to pay for a home body-fat analyser are unknown. Professional demand for clinical accuracy is also uncertain and may not translate to consumer purchases.. Would change if: If the Consumer vs Professional Messaging Test shows the professional group’s purchase intent exceeds the consumer group by at least 10 percentage points, we would shift focus to a B2B expansion.; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for home body-fat measurement in 1993, we would reconsider the investment.; If the pilot reveals low willingness to pay or low purchase intent, we would abandon the consumer proposition and focus on the existing B2B market.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available by late 2002 to justify ACR Electronics investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology.. Constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive landscape for a consumer product.; Must consider ACR’s existing B2B products (shipping, aircraft, military, marine) and its current reach to individual buyers.; Must assess regulatory and market feasibility of a consumer product using satellite distress beacons.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual users (e.g., marine recreational users, outdoor enthusiasts) with a dedicated product line and marketing.; 2) Expand the existing B2B product line into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add a consumer‑focused version of the beacon for marine recreational users).; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B customers and existing product portfolio.; 4) License the 406 MHz technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer products, capturing value through royalties rather than direct consumer sales..

T1: Individual users will adopt a consumer personal locator beacon primarily for marine recreational activities because they need reliable distress signaling in remote areas where cell coverage is absent, and they trust the technology's proven rescue capability. Who benefits: Marine recreational users (boaters, campers, outdoor enthusiasts) who face life-threatening situations at sea.. Why behaviour changes: These users currently lack affordable, reliable ways to signal distress when lost or in danger, and they would switch to a consumer beacon if it is affordable, easy to use, and backed by a rescue track record.. How value is captured: ACR would sell a differentiated consumer product line through marine retailers and online channels, capturing value through premium pricing justified by the rescue capability and brand trust.. Assumptions: Marine recreational users are willing to pay a premium for a reliable distress beacon.; The 406 MHz technology meets or exceeds the FCC's safety and performance standards for consumer use.; ACR can reach these users through existing marine retail channels or new online distribution.. Predictions: Surveyed marine recreational users will indicate intent to purchase a consumer beacon at a price above $50.; Sales of a consumer beacon will be concentrated in regions with high boating activity (e.g., Florida, Alaska).; Competitive products will be priced lower than ACR's proposed consumer line, limiting market share..

T2: Individual users will adopt a consumer personal locator beacon primarily for outdoor emergency preparedness and disaster response, because they need a reliable way to signal distress in remote areas where cell coverage is absent, and they trust the technology's proven rescue capability. Who benefits: Outdoor enthusiasts, campers, hikers, and disaster preparedness enthusiasts who face life-threatening situations in remote environments.. Why behaviour changes: These users currently lack affordable, reliable ways to signal distress when lost or in danger, and they would switch to a consumer beacon if it is affordable, easy to use, and backed by a rescue track record.. How value is captured: ACR would sell a differentiated consumer product line through outdoor and disaster preparedness retailers and online channels, capturing value through premium pricing justified by the rescue capability and brand trust.. Assumptions: Outdoor recreational users are willing to pay a premium for a reliable distress beacon.; The 406 MHz technology meets or exceeds the FCC's safety and performance standards for consumer use.; ACR can reach these users through existing outdoor retail channels or new online distribution.. Predictions: Surveyed outdoor recreational users will indicate intent to purchase a consumer beacon at a price above $50.; Sales of a consumer beacon will be concentrated in regions with high outdoor recreation activity (e.g., national parks, wilderness areas).; Competitive products will be priced lower than ACR's proposed consumer line, limiting market share..

Test "Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Marine vs. Outdoor Recreational Users" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios to measure willingness to pay for a consumer personal locator beacon. Participants are recruited from two target segments: marine recreational users (boaters, campers) and outdoor recreational users (hikers, campers, disaster preparedness enthusiasts). Each participant sees a product description and price, and is asked to indicate their maximum price they would pay.. Sample: Proposed sample: 200 participants (100 marine recreational users, 100 outdoor recreational users), recruited via online panels. Stratified by region (Florida, Alaska, national parks) to reflect high activity areas.. Measure: Maximum price participants would pay for the beacon, and intent to purchase (binary: "Would buy at this price?" or "Would not buy at this price?").. Predictions: T1: Marine recreational users will report willingness to pay at least $50 and higher intent to purchase than outdoor recreational users.; T2: Outdoor recreational users will report willingness to pay at least $50 and higher intent to purchase than marine recreational users.. Decision rule: If the average willingness-to-pay for marine users exceeds that of outdoor users by at least $10 (e.g., $60 vs. $50), proceed with a differentiated marine-focused consumer proposition. If the difference is below $10, proceed with a differentiated outdoor-focused proposition. If both segments show willingness to pay below $50, do not expand.. Cost: 8000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public sources show the 406 MHz PLB is intended for general public use in life-threatening situations, and ACR already sells to marine recreational users. Evidence of willingness to pay and market demand is lacking; run the proposed willingness-to-pay survey before committing. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a warehouse label printer and does not address consumer demand, willingness to pay, or the specific use case of marine recreational users. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public sources show the 406 MHz PLB is intended for general public use in life-threatening situations, and ACR already sells to marine recreational users. Target customer: Marine recreational users (boaters, campers, outdoor enthusiasts) who face life-threatening situations at sea.. Value proposition: A differentiated consumer personal locator beacon that provides reliable distress signaling in remote areas where cell coverage is absent, backed by a rescue track record and affordable pricing.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed willingness-to-pay survey (200 participants, $8,000, 6 weeks) to measure demand and price sensitivity before any product development.. Uncertainty: The size of the marine recreational market, willingness to pay a premium, and ACR's ability to reach these users through existing marine retail channels or new online distribution are uncertain.. Would change if: If the willingness-to-pay survey shows marine users willing to pay at least $50 and higher intent to purchase than outdoor users, proceed with a differentiated marine-focused proposition.; If the survey shows both segments showing willingness to pay below $50, do not expand into consumer products.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.. Constraints: Limited to public sources available up to mid-1962; No access to internal company data or financial figures; Test budget of €20,000 and 12-week timeframe for any proposed experiment; Must consider the existing distribution network of independent dealers and the current reach to individual buyers. Alternatives: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small-scale landscaping, gardening, or light construction); Expand the existing dealer network to reach more individual buyers without a differentiated proposition; Maintain the current business model with no expansion (continue selling through independent dealers); Target a different customer group (e.g., small farms, hobby farmers, or urban property owners) rather than a specific use case.

T1: Households will purchase a differentiated consumer proposition because they view the tractor as a practical, low-cost tool for small-scale tasks, and Deere can capture value by selling a branded, differentiated unit at a premium price through its existing dealer network. Who benefits: Households with small gardens seeking convenient, affordable landscaping solutions. Why behaviour changes: Growing household garden size and awareness of the tractor's versatility make it an attractive, single purchase for chores. How value is captured: Deere earns higher margins by selling a branded, differentiated unit directly to consumers rather than through generic dealer inventory. Assumptions: Households in 1962 have sufficient disposable income for a garden tractor; Deere's engineering reputation justifies a premium price; Deere's dealer network can effectively promote and distribute the consumer proposition. Predictions: Surveyed households will indicate intent to purchase a garden tractor for specific tasks; Sales of a differentiated consumer model will exceed sales of a generic dealer-invented unit; Deere's revenue from consumer sales will be higher than from its farm equipment line.

T2: Households will purchase a differentiated consumer proposition because they view the tractor as a status symbol and utility item, and Deere can capture value by selling a premium-priced, branded unit that signals ownership and convenience. Who benefits: Affluent households and early adopters who seek a status symbol and convenient landscaping solution. Why behaviour changes: Growing middle-class disposable income and the desire to display ownership of modern, convenient equipment create demand for a differentiated, branded unit. How value is captured: Deere earns higher margins by selling a premium-priced, branded unit directly to consumers rather than through generic dealer inventory. Assumptions: Affluent households in 1962 have disposable income to purchase a garden tractor; The tractor's branding and design are perceived as a status symbol; Deere's marketing can effectively communicate the premium value. Predictions: Surveyed households will indicate intent to purchase a garden tractor for status and convenience; Sales of a differentiated consumer model will be concentrated among affluent segments; Deere's revenue from premium-priced consumer sales will be higher than from its farm equipment line.

T1 supports, from deere-wheelhorse-demand (independent_study): "The demand for garden tractors was rapidly increasing as households with small gardens found them rather inexpensive, practical to use for a variety of chores, and they were economical to maintain.". Does not show: It does not show that households would purchase a differentiated proposition, only that garden tractors are seen as practical and affordable..

T2 neutral, from deere-ctf-1959 (company_assertion): "An interesting side note is that in 1959, according to Lee Wannie, who was an engineering department draftsman at John Deere's Horicon plant, a prototype lawn and garden tractor had been built at their factory.". Does not show: It does not address whether households purchase the tractor for status or convenience, nor does it provide evidence of demand for a differentiated proposition..
Looked for evidence against T1: "households do not purchase garden tractors for specific tasks 1962"; found deere-wheelhorse-demand, deere-ctf-1959, deere-ctf-competitive.

Test "Consumer Proposition Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to two product descriptions of a differentiated garden tractor. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a description emphasizing practicality, affordability, and versatility for small-scale tasks; Group B sees a description emphasizing status, branding, and convenience as a modern ownership symbol. Both groups are asked about purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium.. Sample: 400 U.S. households recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and garden ownership, stratified to ensure representation across regions.. Measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum price willing to pay (EUR). Secondary measure: self-reported importance of status vs practicality.. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay a premium than Group B.; T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay a premium than Group A.. Decision rule: If the average willingness to pay in Group A exceeds Group B by at least 15% (e.g., €800 vs €700), we conclude T1 is supported and recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition focused on practicality. If Group B exceeds Group A by at least 15%, we conclude T2 is supported and recommend a premium-priced status-focused proposition. If the difference is <15%, we conclude neither theory is strongly supported and recommend further market research.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for small-scale landscaping, leveraging Deere's existing dealer network to sell a branded, practical garden tractor at a premium price. The evidence shows growing household garden size and the tractor's affordability and versatility, supporting the practical demand hypothesis. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated result concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address household purchase motivations or demand for a differentiated garden tractor. Therefore it provides no evidence for or against T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for small-scale landscaping, leveraging Deere's existing dealer network to sell a branded, practical garden tractor at a premium price. Target customer: Households with small gardens seeking convenient, affordable landscaping solutions. Value proposition: A differentiated garden tractor that combines Deere's engineering reputation with a consumer-friendly design, sold through independent dealers to offer convenience and brand trust.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Preference Test (400 households, two randomized exposure groups, willingness-to-pay threshold of 15% premium) to validate demand for a practical proposition.. Uncertainty: The actual purchase intent and willingness to pay for a differentiated proposition are unknown; the test will resolve this.. Would change if: If the test shows Group B (status-focused) exceeding Group A by at least 15% in purchase intent and willingness to pay, we would shift to a premium-priced status proposition.; If no test result meets the 15% threshold, we would recommend further market research before committing to a differentiated offering.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Lifestyle vs Functional Use Case Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to a hearing protection product described as either (1) a stylish lifestyle accessory marketed for fashion and status, or (2) a functional safety item marketed for a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, medical). Participants indicate willingness to pay, purchase intent, and perceived safety.. Sample: 400 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region to ensure representativeness.. Measure: Willingness to pay (WTP) for each product description, purchase intent (1‑10 scale), and self-reported perceived safety (1‑10 scale).. Predictions: T1: Higher willingness to pay and purchase intent for the lifestyle product compared to the functional product.; T2: Higher willingness to pay and purchase intent for the functional product compared to the lifestyle product.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the lifestyle product is at least 20% higher than for the functional product (i.e., lifestyle WTP ≥ 1.2 × functional WTP) and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), proceed to develop a differentiated lifestyle proposition. If the functional product’s WTP is at least 20% higher, focus on functional positioning. If neither difference is significant, do not invest in a differentiated proposition.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory, targeting health-conscious and status-driven consumers. T1 kept: The simulated result concerns wear comfort and does not address consumer demand for a differentiated lifestyle proposition. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-B.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory, targeting health-conscious and status-driven consumers. Begin with a small-scale online test to validate willingness to pay and purchase intent for a stylish product. Target customer: Health-conscious adults and status-conscious consumers who view hearing protection as a fashion item rather than a functional safety item.. Value proposition: A stylish, design-focused hearing protection product that signals personal style and health awareness, offering premium pricing and brand extension.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Lifestyle vs Functional Use Case Test (400 adults, randomized exposure, WTP and purchase intent measurements) to determine whether willingness to pay for a lifestyle product is at least 20% higher than for a functional use‑. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for a differentiated lifestyle proposition is unknown; willingness to pay for a premium stylish product is uncertain. The test will resolve this uncertainty.. Would change if: If the test shows the functional use‑case product achieving at least 20% higher willingness to pay than the lifestyle product, we would shift focus to a functional positioning strategy.; If the test fails to show a significant difference in willingness to pay between the two product descriptions, we would reconsider the investment in a differentiated proposition.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Home-Studio Creators" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with a choice-based conjoint design. Participants are recruited from home-studio creators and individual producers. They are shown a product description of a Neumann professional microphone and asked to indicate their maximum price they would pay (willingness-to-pay) and to rank importance of three attributes: (1) brand reputation as the industry standard, (2) durability and build quality, and (3) overall sound quality. They also indicate whether they would purchase the product and their likelihood to buy.. Sample: 300 participants: 150 home-studio creators and 150 individual producers, recruited via audio forums, social media, and professional networks.. Measure: Average willingness-to-pay (EUR) for the Neumann microphone, and the proportion of participants who would purchase at each price point. Secondary measure: importance ranking of attributes.. Predictions: T1: Creators will show higher willingness-to-pay for the brand-reputation attribute and lower willingness-to-pay for durability, indicating premium pricing driven by reputation.; T2: Creators will show higher willingness-to-pay for the durability and build-quality attribute and lower willingness-to-pay for brand reputation, indicating premium pricing driven by reliability.. Decision rule: If the average willingness-to-pay for brand reputation exceeds durability by at least 10 percentage points (e.g., 60% vs 50%), conclude T1 is supported. If durability exceeds brand reputation by at least 10 percentage points (e.g., 60% vs 50%), conclude T2 is supported. If neither difference is statistically significant (difference < 10 percentage points), neither theory is strongly supported and further testing is needed.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Develop a differentiated home-studio proposition for individual creators, emphasizing Neumann's brand reputation as the industry standard for professional audio quality. This approach leverages the existing Academy content and the premium positioning already observed in reviews to justify higher pricing and capture value through subscription services. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Develop a differentiated home-studio proposition for individual creators, emphasizing Neumann's brand reputation as the industry standard for professional audio quality. This approach leverages the existing Academy content and the premium positioning already observed in reviews to justify higher pricing and capture value through subscription services. Target customer: Home-studio creators and individual producers who seek high-quality equipment to produce professional-sounding content.. Value proposition: Position Neumann as the gold standard for professional audio quality, offering premium pricing justified by brand reputation and ongoing support through the Home Studio Academy.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed willingness-to-pay survey (300 participants, 8 weeks, €18,000) to test the brand-reputation vs. durability premium. Use the decision rule: if brand reputation exceeds durability by ≥10 percentage points, proceed with the T1. Uncertainty: The willingness of individual creators to pay a premium for brand reputation is uncertain. Economic constraints and price sensitivity of home-studio buyers are also unknown.. Would change if: If the survey shows durability exceeding brand reputation by ≥10 percentage points, we would shift to T2 and prioritize durability positioning.; If the willingness-to-pay for brand reputation is below 50% or the premium is not statistically significant, we would reconsider the differentiated proposition and explore other alternatives.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Lifestyle vs Medical Messaging Willingness-to-Pay Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with random assignment to one of two product descriptions and a choice of price. Participants are recruited via panels to match demographic characteristics of the target segments.. Sample: 400 participants: 200 general consumers (age 18-45) and 200 consumers with self-reported hearing sensitivity (age 18-45). Randomly assigned to either lifestyle or medical messaging.. Measure: Maximum willingness-to-pay (WTP) for a hearing protector described in the assigned message, and binary purchase intent (yes/no).. Predictions: T1: General consumers will show higher WTP and purchase intent when the message emphasizes lifestyle and outdoor activities (lifestyle group).; T2: Consumers with hearing sensitivity will show higher WTP and purchase intent when the message emphasizes medical certification and hearing protection as a health safeguard (medical group).. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the lifestyle group exceeds the average WTP for the medical group by at least 10% (e.g., lifestyle WTP >= medical WTP + 10%) and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), we conclude T1 is more supported. If the medical group exceeds the lifestyle group by at least 10% and the difference is statistically significant, we conclude T2 is more supported. Test "Boat Owner vs Safety-Conscious Consumer Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Recruit two groups: (1) private boat owners (n=200) and (2) safety-conscious consumers (n=200). Each group views a product description of an ACR marine safety beacon priced at $700. Boat owners receive a marine safety scenario; safety-conscious consumers receive a general safety scenario. Both groups indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1-7).. Sample: 400 respondents (200 boat owners, 200 safety-conscious consumers) from the US, recruited via marine and outdoor safety forums.. Measure: Purchase intent score for each group on the 7-point scale.. Predictions: T1: Boat owners will show higher purchase intent than safety-conscious consumers.; T2: Safety-conscious consumers will show higher purchase intent than boat owners.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for boat owners is at least 1.5 points higher than for safety-conscious consumers, proceed to develop a marine safety proposition. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, do not commit to a consumer proposition and conduct further research.. Cost: 12000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not commit to a consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows ACR's technology is approved for general public use and is already sold to commercial marine users, but it does not demonstrate that private boat owners will purchase a marine safety beacon or that they are willing to pay a premium price. Conduct the proposed purchase intent test to measure demand before investing. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence about a label printer reducing packing errors does not address consumer demand for a marine safety beacon, so it does not affect T1. New claim: Private boat owners will adopt a consumer distress-beacon product because they face high personal risk in open water and already use portable emergency equipment, so a differentiated marine safety proposition will generate demand.. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows ACR's technology is approved for general public use and is already sold to commercial marine users, but it does not demonstrate that private boat owners will purchase a marine safety beacon or that they are willing to pay a premium price. Conduct the proposed purchase intent test to measure demand before investing. Target customer: Private boat owners and their owners who need reliable emergency communication in open water.. Value proposition: A differentiated marine safety beacon that integrates with existing portable equipment, positioned as a reliable distress signal for life-threatening situations.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the online purchase intent test (400 respondents, 8 weeks, €12,000) to compare boat owner and safety-conscious consumer purchase intent.. Uncertainty: Demand for a marine safety beacon among private boat owners and willingness to pay a premium price are unknown. The test will resolve this uncertainty.. Would change if: If the test shows boat owners' purchase intent is at least 1.5 points higher than safety-conscious consumers, we would proceed to develop a marine safety proposition.; If the test shows no significant difference or lower intent, we would reconsider expansion and explore other alternatives.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory that enhances outdoor activities and personal safety. Who benefits: Consumers seeking comfort and style during outdoor recreation and work; Hellberg Safety gains premium pricing and brand equity.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers view hearing protection as a fashion item and a status symbol, they will purchase multiple pairs and be willing to pay a premium for comfort and design.. How value is captured: Hellberg can charge higher prices for differentiated designs, sell through specialty retailers or direct-to-consumer channels, and capture value through brand loyalty and repeat purchases.. Assumptions: Consumers associate hearing protection with outdoor lifestyle and personal safety.; There is a market segment willing to pay a premium for comfort and design.; Hellberg can design and market a differentiated product without compromising safety standards.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% more for a hearing protector marketed as a lifestyle accessory.; Purchase intent will be higher for a product marketed with visible design features compared to a standard earplug.; Repeat purchase rate will be higher for a differentiated product than for a generic earplug..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive hearing protection as a medical necessity for specific health risks (e.g., noise-induced hearing loss). Who benefits: Consumers with hearing sensitivity; Hellberg Safety gains premium pricing and brand credibility as a safety leader.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers view hearing protection as a health requirement, they will purchase specialized products and be willing to pay higher prices for proven protection.. How value is captured: Hellberg can price differentiated products at premium levels, sell through medical and specialty retailers, and capture value through health-focused marketing and certifications.. Assumptions: Consumers with hearing sensitivity are aware of hearing protection as a medical necessity.; There is a market segment willing to pay a premium for medical-grade hearing protection.; Hellberg can design and market a differentiated product that meets medical standards without compromising safety.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers with hearing sensitivity will indicate willingness to pay at least 30% more for a hearing protector marketed as medical essential.; Purchase intent will be higher for a product marketed with medical certifications compared to a standard earplug.; Repeat purchase rate will be higher for a differentiated product than for a generic earplug..

Test "Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Lifestyle vs Medical Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 500 adults recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region to reflect Europe. 250 participants will receive a lifestyle message (e.g., "Peace of Mind for Outdoor Adventures"), and 250 will receive a medical necessity message (e.g., "Proven Protection for Noise-Induced Hearing Loss").. Measure: WTP for a differentiated hearing protector priced at €50 (€25 for lifestyle, €25 for medical). Secondary measure: self-reported likelihood to purchase (1‑10 scale).. Predictions: T1: Higher WTP for the lifestyle message (average ≥ 25) and higher purchase intent for the lifestyle message compared to the medical message.; T2: Higher WTP for the medical necessity message (average ≥ 25) and higher purchase intent for the medical message compared to the lifestyle message.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the lifestyle message is at least 25 and significantly higher than the medical message (p < 0.05), proceed with a differentiated lifestyle proposition. If the average WTP for the medical message is at least 25 and significantly higher than the lifestyle message, proceed with a differentiated medical proposition. If both WTPs are below 20 (or difference < 5 points), no expansion is justified.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting outdoor recreation and lifestyle users, using comfort and design as key differentiators. Begin with a limited launch of a premium hearing protector marketed as a lifestyle accessory, sold through specialty retailers and direct-to-consumer channels. Use the proposed willingness-to-pay survey to validate demand before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-B shows that a softer, better-fitting protector did not increase wear frequency compared to a standard one. This contradicts T1, which predicts higher willingness to wear a differentiated lifestyle product. Therefore T1 is rejected. New claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive hearing protection as a medical necessity for specific health risks (e.g., noise-induced hearing loss).. Evidence: SYN-B.

Group B sees a convenience‑focused message: 'Get an instant one‑button body‑fat measurement for quick health tracking.' Both groups see a price point of €199 for a basic home scale. Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10) and the primary reason they would buy.. Sample: 400 adults aged 18‑95 in the United States, screened for health concern and willingness to pay for a home scale.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and primary reason for purchase (open‑ended).. Predictions: T1: Group A will have higher purchase intent and more participants citing health risk reduction as the primary reason.; T2: Group B will have higher purchase intent and more participants citing convenience/ease of use as the primary reason.. Decision rule: If the difference in average purchase intent between the two groups is ≥ 1.5 points and Group A’s intent is at least 1.5 points higher, proceed to develop a health‑focused consumer proposition. If the difference is ≤ 1.5 points and Group B’s intent is at least 1.5 points higher, develop a convenience‑focused proposition. If the difference is ≤ 1.5 points and Group A’s intent is at least 1.5 points higher, no expansion is recommended.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows Tanita already has a validated clinic/health-club body-fat analyser and a strong commercial presence, but it does not show consumer demand for a health-focused home device. A small, low-cost test (as proposed) is needed to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows Tanita already has a validated clinic/health-club body-fat analyser and a strong commercial presence, but it does not show consumer demand for a health-focused home device. A small, low-cost test (as proposed) is needed to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent before committing resources. Target customer: Health-conscious consumers aged 18‑95 who are motivated to reduce disease risk and are willing to pay for evidence-based body-fat results.. Uncertainty: Consumer willingness to pay for a health‑focused device and actual purchase behavior are unknown; the test will resolve this.. Would change if: If the test shows a ≥ 1.5 point difference in purchase intent between the health‑focused and convenience‑focused groups, the recommendation would shift accordingly.; If the test shows no significant difference or the convenience group wins, no expansion would be recommended.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Test "Consumer Messaging Test: Lifestyle vs Compliance" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from two distinct groups: Lifestyle Group (n=300) and Compliance Group (n=300). Both groups are then asked about purchase intent and willingness to pay.. Sample: 300 consumers, 150 per group, recruited via an online panel to ensure geographic diversity.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would purchase) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR). Secondary measure: stated primary use case (lifestyle vs compliance).. Predictions: T1: Lifestyle Group will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Compliance Group.; T2: Compliance Group will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Lifestyle Group.. Decision rule: If the average willingness to pay of the Lifestyle Group exceeds the average willingness to pay of the Compliance Group by at least €10, proceed with a differentiated lifestyle proposition. An interesting side note is that in 1959, according to Lee Wannie, who was an engineering department draftsman at John Deere’s Horicon plant, a prototype lawn and garden tractor had been built at their factory.
Deere had purchased several competitive lawn and garden tractors to make evaluations on pros and cons of each brand.

Lawn and garden equipment sales rise 76 percent.

Test "Consumer Choice Experiment: Lifestyle vs Medical Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice experiment with between‑subjects design. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Lifestyle Condition (message emphasizing comfort, style, and outdoor lifestyle appeal) or Medical Condition (message emphasizing hearing protection as a medical necessity and health protection). Participants view a product description of a differentiated hearing protector (e.g., a comfortable, stylish earplug) and are asked to indicate willingness to pay (WTP) and likelihood to purchase on a 7‑point scale.. Sample: 300 adults aged 18–65, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and age to reflect the target consumer segment.. Measure: WTP (price participants would pay) and purchase intent (likelihood to buy on 7‑point scale).. Predictions: T1: Participants in the Lifestyle Condition will report higher WTP and purchase intent than those in the Medical Condition.; T2: Participants in the Medical Condition will report higher WTP and purchase intent than those in the Lifestyle Condition.. Decision rule: If the average WTP in the Lifestyle Condition exceeds the average WTP in the Medical Condition by at least €15 (or a ≥ 15% increase), we conclude there is sufficient evidence for a differentiated lifestyle proposition. If the Medical Condition shows a ≥ 15% higher WTP, we conclude there is sufficient evidence for a medical‑focused proposition. If neither difference meets the threshold, we conclude insufficient evidence to justify investment.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory for outdoor recreation and personal safety, rather than a medical necessity. Test "Consumer Messaging Test: Safety vs Trust Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Run a controlled online experiment with two identical product pages for a Jotun marine protective coating (e.g., marine hull primer). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two messaging conditions: (A) Safety-focused messaging emphasizing marine-grade protection, durability, and safety certifications; (B) Trust-focused messaging emphasizing Jotun's long-standing marine expertise, safety reputation, and proven performance. Both pages include the same product price and availability. Track click-through rate and purchase intent (binary: "Would buy this product?").. Sample: 500 adult respondents in Scandinavia and North America, screened for boat ownership or outdoor equipment use.. Measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage of participants who click "Would buy this product?" for the respective condition).. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent in the safety-focused condition.; T2: Higher purchase intent in the trust-focused condition.. Decision rule: If the safety-focused condition achieves at least 15% higher purchase intent than the trust-focused condition, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing safety and durability (support T1). If the trust-focused condition achieves at least 15% higher purchase intent, proceed with a consumer proposition emphasizing brand trust and marine expertise (support T2). If neither condition meets the 15% threshold, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows Jotun already sells directly to individual buyers and has a consumer presence, but it does not prove that consumers are motivated by safety and durability. the impedance value of a body to be measured vary according to the date, time and differences of body condition before measurement. These various are too large to use the above-described inference formula accurately and amount of body fat calculated by the formula is likely to be inaccurate.

This method is safe, noninvasive, provides rapid measurements, requires little operator skill and subject cooperation, and is portable. Further validation of this method is recommended in subjects with abnormal body composition.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in 1993 to justify Tanita investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its stand‑on bioelectrical impedance body‑fat analyser, by evaluating demand, market fit, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.. Constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; no internal company data.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Evidence must address consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning; no financial data available.; Any recommendation must be based on observable market behavior, not speculation about future outcomes.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home users for a specific use case (e.g., weight management, fitness tracking).; 2) Expand the existing B2B offering by adding new features or marketing channels to clinics and health clubs without a consumer focus.; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B market (clinics and health clubs).; 4) License the technology to third‑party manufacturers to create consumer devices, capturing value through royalties rather than direct sales..

Who benefits: Jotun benefits by capturing premium pricing and repeat purchases from individual buyers who seek reliable marine protection.. Why behaviour changes: Buyers shift from generic or cheaper alternatives to Jotun when they trust the brand’s reputation for marine performance and safety, and when they need protection for their boats.. Test "Digital Messaging Test for Jotun Consumer Proposition" between T1; T2. Method: Run a targeted online ad campaign with two identical landing pages offering a limited-time discount on a Jotun marine coating product. Track conversion rate (purchase or sign-up) and post‑purchase survey questions about trust in the brand and lifestyle alignment.. Sample: Estimated 5,000 unique visitors (2,000 per ad variant) from a panel of individual boat owners and marine enthusiasts in Scandinavia and the Nordics.. Measure: Conversion rate (purchase or sign‑up) and average self‑reported trust score (1‑10) and lifestyle alignment score (1‑10) from post‑purchase survey.. Predictions: T1: Higher conversion rate and higher trust score for the variant emphasizing trust in the brand (Jotun’s marine reputation).; T2: Higher conversion rate and higher lifestyle alignment score for the variant emphasizing lifestyle and sustainability values.. Decision rule: If the variant emphasizing trust (T1) achieves a conversion rate at least 15 percentage points higher than the variant emphasizing lifestyle (T2) AND the average trust score is at least 2 points higher, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition focused on trust. If the lifestyle variant beats trust by at least 15 points and trust is not significantly higher, prioritize lifestyle. If neither threshold is met, do not invest.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows Jotun already offers direct consumer sales and serves DIY customers, but it does not prove that individual buyers choose Jotun because of trust in the brand. Test "Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Lifestyle vs Medical Proposition" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to a lifestyle marketing message versus a medical marketing message, followed by a willingness-to-pay (WTP) question.. Sample: 500 adults recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and region to reflect Europe. Stratify by hearing sensitivity (self-reported) to test T2.. Measure: WTP in euros for a hearing protector marketed as (a) a lifestyle accessory with visible design (e.g., color, pattern) and (b) a medical necessity with visible EN 352 certification.. Predictions: T1: Higher WTP for lifestyle proposition, especially among non-hearing-sensitive participants.; T2: Higher WTP for medical proposition, especially among participants who self-report hearing sensitivity.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the lifestyle proposition exceeds the average WTP for the medical proposition by at least €10, proceed with developing a differentiated consumer proposition targeting lifestyle. If the difference is less than €10, do not invest in a differentiated proposition.. Cost: 15000 euros, 12 weeks.

Predictions: T1: Dedicated lawn tractor will be chosen by ≥60% of households; versatile lawn tractor by <20%.; T2: Versatile lawn tractor will be chosen by ≥60% of households; dedicated lawn tractor by <20%.. Decision rule: If dedicated lawn tractor share ≥60% and versatile lawn tractor share <20%, conclude T1 is supported. If versatile lawn tractor share ≥60% and dedicated lawn tractor share <20%, conclude T2 is supported. If both shares <20%, inconclusive. If both share ≥20%, incon. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

T1: Private boat owners will adopt a consumer distress-beacon if it is marketed as a marine safety necessity, because they face higher emergency risks and are willing to pay a premium for reliable communication. Test "Consumer vs Agency Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated product descriptions and purchase price options.. Sample: 500 respondents: 250 private boat owners (recruited via marine forums and social media) and 250 emergency service providers (recruited via industry associations).. Measure: Willingness to pay (WTP) for a 406 MHz beacon and purchase intent (binary: would buy).. Predictions: T1: Private boat owners will show higher WTP and purchase intent than emergency service providers.; T2: Emergency service providers will show higher WTP and purchase intent than private boat owners.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for private boat owners exceeds that for emergency service providers by at least 10% (e.g., $150 vs $135), proceed with a consumer proposition targeting marine safety. If the difference is less than 10%, do not invest in a consumer proposition and focus on B2B.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows ACR's technology is approved for general public use and has been sold to marine users, but it does not demonstrate consumer demand or willingness to pay a premium. Conduct the proposed purchase intent test to measure actual demand before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows ACR's technology is approved for general public use and has been sold to marine users, but it does not demonstrate consumer demand or willingness to pay a premium. Conduct the proposed purchase intent test to measure actual demand before committing resources. Target customer: Private boat owners and their owners who need reliable emergency communication.. Value proposition: A marine-specific 406 MHz distress-beacon marketed as a low-cost, self-contained safety solution for boats, leveraging ACR's existing marine reputation and regulatory approval.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the Consumer vs Agency Purchase Intent Test (online survey with simulated product descriptions and purchase price options) to compare willingness to pay and purchase intent between private boat owners and emergency service providers.. Uncertainty: Consumer demand and willingness to pay a premium for a marine beacon remain uncertain; the test will resolve this.. Would change if: If the test shows private boat owners' average willingness to pay exceeds emergency service providers' by at least 10%, we would proceed with a consumer proposition targeting marine safety.; If the test shows no significant difference or emergency service providers show higher willingness to pay, we would reconsider investment and focus on B2B or licensing.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1: Consumers will adopt a stand‑on body‑fat analyser for home use if they perceive it as a health‑monitoring tool that provides measurable, reliable body‑fat data, because they value evidence‑based health decisions. Why behaviour changes: If consumers learn that the device measures body fat with a validated method (e.g., Tanita’s 0.8 kg bias relative to a four‑compartment model), they will be motivated to purchase it for personal health tracking.. How value is captured: Tanita can capture value by selling the device at a premium price justified by its accuracy and by licensing the technology to other consumer brands for health‑tracking features.. Assumptions: Consumers trust medical‑grade accuracy when they see a validated measurement method.; Health‑conscious consumers are willing to pay a premium for a device that provides measurable body‑fat data.; The device can be marketed as a health‑monitoring tool rather than just a scale.. Predictions: If a survey of health‑conscious consumers shows >30% would purchase a stand‑on BIA analyser for home use, the theory is supported.; If a controlled test shows purchase intent increases when accuracy is highlighted, the theory is supported.; If a competitor launches a similar device without accuracy claims, consumer demand may be limited..

T2: Consumers will adopt a stand‑on body‑fat analyser for home use if they perceive it as a convenient, non‑invasive health monitoring tool that fits their lifestyle, because they value time‑saving and ease of use. Who benefits: Consumers seeking a quick, at‑home health check without the hassle of clinic visits or multiple devices.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers learn the device provides rapid, reliable body‑fat measurement and can be used in the privacy of their home, they will be motivated to purchase it for daily health tracking.. How value is captured: Tanita can capture value by selling the device at a premium price justified by its speed and convenience, and by licensing the technology to other consumer brands for health‑tracking features.. Assumptions: Consumers prioritize convenience and speed over accuracy when choosing health monitoring tools.; The device can be marketed as a time‑saving, at‑home solution rather than a medical tool.; There is a market segment willing to pay for a device that fits their lifestyle.. Predictions: If a survey of health‑conscious consumers shows >30% would purchase a stand‑on BIA analyser for home use, the theory is supported.; If a controlled test shows purchase intent increases when convenience is highlighted, the theory is supported.; If a competitor launches a similar device without convenience claims, consumer demand may be limited..

Measure: 1) Purchase intent on a 1‑10 scale (1‑very unlikely, 10‑very likely). 2) WTP in euros for a stand‑on BIA analyser (median value). 3) Self‑reported importance of accuracy vs. convenience vs. other factors..
