T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory that enhances outdoor activities and personal safety. Who benefits: Consumers seeking comfort and style during outdoor recreation and work; Hellberg Safety gains premium pricing and brand equity.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers view hearing protection as a fashion item and a status symbol, they will purchase multiple pairs and be willing to pay a premium for comfort and design.. How value is captured: Hellberg can charge higher prices for differentiated designs, sell through specialty retailers or direct-to-consumer channels, and capture value through brand loyalty and repeat purchases.. Assumptions: Consumers associate hearing protection with outdoor lifestyle and personal safety.; There is a market segment willing to pay a premium for comfort and design.; Hellberg can design and market a differentiated product without compromising safety standards.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% more for a hearing protector marketed as a lifestyle accessory.; Purchase intent will be higher for a product marketed with visible design features compared to a standard earplug.; Repeat purchase rate will be higher for a differentiated product than for a generic earplug..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive hearing protection as a medical necessity for specific health risks (e.g., noise-induced hearing loss). Who benefits: Consumers with hearing sensitivity; Hellberg Safety gains premium pricing and brand credibility as a safety leader.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers view hearing protection as a health requirement, they will purchase specialized products and be willing to pay higher prices for proven protection.. How value is captured: Hellberg can price differentiated products at premium levels, sell through medical and specialty retailers, and capture value through health-focused marketing and certifications.. Assumptions: Consumers with hearing sensitivity are aware of hearing protection as a medical necessity.; There is a market segment willing to pay a premium for medical-grade hearing protection.; Hellberg can design and market a differentiated product that meets medical standards without compromising safety.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers with hearing sensitivity will indicate willingness to pay at least 30% more for a hearing protector marketed as medical essential.; Purchase intent will be higher for a product marketed with medical certifications compared to a standard earplug.; Repeat purchase rate will be higher for a differentiated product than for a generic earplug..

Test "Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Lifestyle vs Medical Proposition" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to either a lifestyle-focused proposition (e.g., 'Hearing protection as a comfortable outdoor accessory that enhances your experience') or a medical-focused proposition (e.g., 'Hearing protection as a medical necessity for noise-sensitive individuals'). Participants are randomly assigned to view the respective proposition and then asked about maximum price they would pay for a product that meets the stated claim.. Sample: 500 adults aged 18-55, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and geographic region to reflect Europe. 250 participants exposed to lifestyle proposition, 250 exposed to medical proposition.. Measure: Maximum price participants would pay for a product that matches the stated claim (in euros).. Predictions: T1: Higher maximum price for lifestyle proposition (average €45) than for medical proposition (average €35).; T2: Higher maximum price for medical proposition (average €45) than for lifestyle proposition (average €35).. Decision rule: If the difference in average maximum price between lifestyle and medical propositions is at least €10, proceed to develop a differentiated proposition aligned with the higher price point. If the difference is less than €10, no further investment is justified at this time.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory for outdoor recreation and personal safety, rather than as a medical necessity. Use the proposed willingness-to-pay survey to validate demand before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-B shows that a softer, better-fitting protector did not increase wear frequency compared to a standard one. This contradicts T1's prediction that comfort and design would drive higher adoption. Therefore T1 is not supported by this evidence. New claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive hearing protection as a medical necessity for specific health risks (e.g., noise-induced hearing loss).. Evidence: SYN-B.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory for outdoor recreation and personal safety, rather than as a medical necessity. Use the proposed willingness-to-pay survey to validate demand before committing resources. Target customer: Outdoor enthusiasts, hikers, cyclists, and consumers who value comfort and style during recreational activities.. Value proposition: A hearing protector designed with comfort, ergonomic fit, and visible design features that enhances outdoor experiences while meeting safety standards, allowing premium pricing and brand differentiation.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the willingness-to-pay survey (500 participants, 10 weeks, €15,000 budget) to measure price sensitivity to lifestyle vs medical messaging.. Uncertainty: The size of the lifestyle market and willingness to pay a premium for comfort and design are uncertain. Evidence SYN-B shows comfort improvements do not increase wear frequency, contradicting T1's core assumption.. Would change if: If the survey shows a price difference of at least €10 between lifestyle and medical propositions, indicating strong demand for a lifestyle proposition, we would proceed to develop a differentiated lifestyle offering.; If new evidence demonstrates that medical necessity drives purchase decisions (e.g., higher willingness to pay for medical messaging), we would shift focus to a medical proposition.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Who benefits: Hellberg Safety would benefit from higher margins and brand extension into consumer markets.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers currently view hearing protection as a functional necessity for work or safety. If they shift perception to a lifestyle accessory, they will be willing to purchase multiple units for different activities (e.g., hiking, music, DIY). How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value through premium pricing, bundled product offerings, and direct-to-consumer sales channels that leverage its design reputation.. Assumptions: Consumers associate hearing protection with lifestyle and performance; There is a measurable willingness to pay for a differentiated consumer proposition; Hellberg can effectively communicate the lifestyle value of its products. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate intent to purchase multiple units for different activities; Sales of a differentiated consumer line will exceed baseline expectations for a single use case; Premium pricing will be accepted by a significant segment of target consumers.

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive hearing protection as a safety requirement for specific high-risk activities (e.g., construction, industrial, outdoor recreation) where compliance is mandatory, leading to repeat purchases and regulatory-driven demand. Who benefits: Hellberg Safety would benefit from increased sales volume, repeat purchases, and potential licensing or certification partnerships.. Why behaviour changes: Regulatory bodies and employers require hearing protection for certain workplaces and activities. If consumers view the product as a compliance necessity, they will purchase it for each use case rather than a one-time purchase.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value through bulk sales to employers, compliance-focused marketing, and potential licensing of its technology to third-party safety products.. Assumptions: Regulatory requirements for hearing protection exist for specific activities; Consumers are aware of and comply with these requirements; Hellberg can meet or exceed the required standards for these use cases. Predictions: Sales of a differentiated consumer line will be driven by B2B purchases from employers and safety contractors; Repeat purchase rates will be higher for activities with mandatory hearing protection; Compliance-driven demand will outweigh lifestyle-driven demand in the target segments.

Test "Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Lifestyle vs Risk-Specific Proposition" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging and choice-based conjoint design. Sample: 500 adult consumers recruited via panel, balanced across gender and age, with a sub-group of 200 who have experienced a loud music event (to test T2) and 200 who have not. Measure: 1) Maximum willingness-to-pay (WTP) for a lifestyle-oriented hearing protection product (design, comfort, multiple use cases) 2) Maximum WTP for a risk-specific product (e.g., concert, hunting) 3) Purchase intent on a 7-point scale. Predictions: T1: Higher average WTP for the lifestyle product and higher purchase intent among those who experienced loud music events; T2: Higher average WTP for the risk-specific product and higher purchase intent among those who experienced loud music events than among those who did not. Decision rule: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition if the average WTP for the lifestyle product exceeds the WTP for the risk-specific product by at least 15% and the difference is statistically significant (p<0.05). If the opposite holds, do not expand.. Cost: 8000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public evidence shows Hellberg already sells to individual buyers and has a consumer line (Junior), but no source demonstrates that consumers perceive hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory or would purchase multiple pairs for different activities. T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated hearing-protection product if it is marketed as a lifestyle accessory that combines comfort, style, and social acceptance, because they currently view hearing protection as utilitarian and appear as a medical necessity. Who benefits: Consumers seeking comfortable, discreet protection for recreational and social activities.. Why behaviour changes: If the product is presented as fashion-forward and socially acceptable, consumers will be willing to switch from standard earplugs to a differentiated offering.. How value is captured: Hellberg can charge a premium price for a stylish, comfortable product and sell through retail channels, capturing value through brand differentiation and higher margins.. Assumptions: Consumers currently perceive hearing protection as a medical necessity rather than a lifestyle item.; Style and comfort are important purchase drivers for recreational use.; Retail distribution is accessible to individual buyers.. Predictions: In a test offering a stylish, comfortable hearing protection product to recreational users, purchase intent will be higher than for standard earplugs.; Willingness to pay will be above the price of standard earplugs when the product is positioned as a lifestyle accessory..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated hearing-protection product if it is marketed as a safety requirement for specific high-risk activities (e.g., construction, hunting, medical), because they already use hearing protection in those environments and trust the certification. Who benefits: Professional and recreational users in high-risk environments who need reliable protection.. Why behaviour changes: If the product is positioned as a mandatory safety item for a specific use case, users will adopt it because they already use hearing protection and trust the certification.. Test "Home-Studio Creator Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with a choice-based conjoint design. Participants are recruited from home-studio creators (self-identified) who have purchased at least one Neumann product in the past 12 months. They are shown two product concepts: (A) a differentiated home-studio line positioned as a professional standard (e.g., lower-cost, specialized features, limited edition). (B) a generic consumer line (identical to existing professional line). Participants indicate their willingness to pay (EUR) and purchase intent (1‑10 scale).. Sample: 300 creators, recruited via home-studio forums, social media, and industry groups. Stratify by experience level (beginner vs. professional) and geographic region to capture diverse perspectives.. Measure: 1) Willingness to pay (EUR) for the differentiated home-studio line. 2) Purchase intent (1‑10) for the differentiated home-studio line. 3) Difference in willingness to pay between the two concepts.. Predictions: T1: Higher willingness to pay and purchase intent for the differentiated home-studio line than for the generic consumer line.; T2: Higher willingness to pay and purchase intent for the generic consumer line than for the differentiated home-studio line.. Decision rule: If the differentiated home-studio line yields a willingness to pay at least 20% higher than the generic consumer line and a purchase intent at least 15 percentage points higher, proceed to develop a differentiated home-studio proposition. If the generic line outperforms, keep the single professional range.. Cost: 15000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Develop a differentiated home-studio proposition for individual creators, positioning Neumann as a professional standard brand. The evidence shows the home-studio market is growing and creators value credibility, but it does not prove they purchase Neumann specifically because of professional perception. Therefore, the recommendation is to test demand for a differentiated line before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Home-Studio Creator Purchase Intent Test (or a smaller pilot) to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent for a differentiated home-studio line versus a generic consumer line.. The test will clarify whether creators are willing to pay more for a differentiated proposition.. Would change if: If the test shows the generic consumer line outperforms the differentiated home-studio line in willingness to pay and purchase intent, or if price sensitivity is high, the recommendation would shift to keep a single professional range for; all customers.. T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated lawn tractor proposition because they view it as a convenient, single‑tool solution for small‑scale landscaping and homeowner tasks, reducing the need to purchase multiple tools. Who benefits: Homeowners and small‑scale gardeners who need a single, versatile machine for mowing, weeding, and light cleanup.. Why behaviour changes: The increasing availability of garden tractors at lower prices and the convenience of a single tool make it attractive to consumers who previously had to buy separate mowers, rakes, and other attachments.. How value is captured: Deere can capture value by selling a differentiated model at a premium price, leveraging its tractor engineering to offer superior performance and durability, and by building brand awareness in the consumer market.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a single, integrated tool.; The market for small‑scale landscaping is growing sufficiently to support a differentiated proposition.; Deere can differentiate its product through design, performance, and brand positioning.. Predictions: A test offering a differentiated lawn tractor to homeowners will generate higher purchase intent and higher conversion rates compared to a standard garden attachment.; Sales of the differentiated model will be concentrated among homeowners with small gardens, not large commercial users..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated lawn tractor proposition because they seek a premium, brand‑reliable product that signals status and quality, leading them to purchase a single, high‑performance machine rather than multiple lower‑cost tools. Who benefits: Affluent homeowners and early adopters who value brand prestige and are willing to pay a premium for a perceived superior product.. Why behaviour changes: The growing consumer market for garden equipment creates an opportunity for Deere to capture premium pricing by positioning its lawn tractor as a high‑performance, brand‑reliable tool, distinct from generic garden attachments.. How value is captured: Deere can capture value by selling a differentiated model at a premium price, leveraging its brand reputation and engineering credibility to justify higher margins and build loyalty among early adopters.. Assumptions: Consumers associate brand reputation with product quality and performance.; The premium price is acceptable to a segment of homeowners willing to invest in a single, high‑performance tool.; Deere can effectively communicate brand value through marketing and distribution channels.. Predictions: A test offering a differentiated lawn tractor to affluent homeowners will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium compared to a standard garden attachment.; Sales of the differentiated model will be concentrated among homeowners with higher disposable income, not the average consumer..

Test "Consumer Proposition Test: Single vs Premium Lawn Tractor" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to a differentiated lawn tractor proposition. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a standard garden attachment description and is asked about purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium; Group B sees a differentiated lawn tractor description emphasizing single, integrated functionality and premium pricing. Both groups are asked the same final question: "Would you purchase this differentiated lawn tractor at a premium price?". Sample: 300 homeowners with small gardens, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and prior garden equipment ownership.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would purchase) and willingness to pay a premium (willingness-to-pay scale).. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium than Group B.; T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium than Group A.. Decision rule: If Group B's purchase intent exceeds Group A's by at least 10 percentage points, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If Group A's purchase intent exceeds Group B's by at least 10 percentage points, maintain the current B2B2C model. If the difference is within 10 points, conduct a smaller follow-up survey to validate the results before committing resources.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for small-scale landscaping and homeowner tasks, leveraging Deere’s tractor engineering. The evidence shows existing lawn tractor capability (1959 prototype, 1963 production, 1960‑91960 sales rise) and a growing consumer market for garden equipment. A test should first measure purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium to validate demand before committing full B2C Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for small-scale landscaping and homeowner tasks, leveraging Deere’s tractor engineering. The evidence shows existing lawn tractor capability (1959 prototype, 1963 production, 1960‑91960 sales rise) and a growing consumer market for garden equipment. A test should first measure purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium to validate demand before committing full B2C Target customer: Homeowners with small gardens who need a single, versatile tool for mowing, weeding, and light cleanup.. Value proposition: A differentiated lawn tractor that combines Deere’s engineering expertise with a single, integrated solution, offering superior performance, durability, and brand reliability at a premium price.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Test (300 homeowners, 8 weeks, €15,000) to compare purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium between a standard garden attachment description and a differentiated lawn tractor description.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for small-scale landscaping and the willingness of homeowners to pay a premium for a differentiated proposition are uncertain. The test will resolve these uncertainties.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent for the differentiated proposition is significantly lower than for a standard garden attachment, we would reconsider the investment and focus on the existing B2B2C model.; If the test shows strong willingness to pay a premium, we would proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition.; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for premium-priced lawn tractors, we would reconsider the premium positioning.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Home-studio creators value professional-grade equipment because it enables consistent, high-quality recordings that are essential for career advancement and audience engagement. Who benefits: Home-studio creators who need reliable gear to produce professional-sounding content.. Why behaviour changes: If creators perceive Neumann as the gold standard, they will be willing to pay a premium for its microphones and monitors, and may purchase multiple units to maintain consistent sound quality.. How value is captured: Neumann can capture value through premium pricing, higher-margin sales, and brand loyalty that encourages repeat purchases.. Assumptions: Creators currently use lower-cost gear that lacks professional sound quality.; They are aware of Neumann's reputation and are willing to invest in it.; There is a measurable willingness to pay for professional-grade equipment.. Predictions: If offered a differentiated home-studio proposition, creators will express higher intent to purchase and be willing to pay a premium over existing professional pricing.; Surveyed creators will rank Neumann higher than competitors in terms of sound quality and professional credibility..

T2: Home-studio creators prioritize convenience and ease of use because they lack time and expertise to manage professional-grade equipment, and Neumann's user-friendly interface and integrated solutions reduce setup time and technical barriers. Who benefits: Home-studio creators who need quick, hassle-free setup and reliable performance without deep technical knowledge.. Why behaviour changes: If creators find Neumann's interface intuitive and its setup simple, they will adopt it over more complex competitors, leading to higher purchase rates and repeat purchases.. How value is captured: Neumann can capture value through lower average order value (AOV) from individual buyers, higher repeat purchase rates, and brand perception as accessible, which can be leveraged for premium pricing.. Assumptions: Creators currently spend significant time troubleshooting or learning to use professional equipment.; They value speed and simplicity in their workflow.; They are willing to pay for a product that reduces setup time and technical barriers.. Predictions: If offered a differentiated home-studio proposition emphasizing ease of use, creators will show higher purchase intent and be willing to pay a premium compared to a standard professional range.; Surveyed creators will rank Neumann higher for ease of use than competitors in terms of time saved and technical simplicity..

Test "Home-Studio Creator Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated product offer and choice-based conjoint. Sample: 300 self-identified home-studio creators (recruited via audio forum panels and social media) who have spent €500+ on audio gear in the past 12 months. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (WTP) in euros. Predictions: T1: Creators exposed to professional-grade proposition will show higher purchase intent and WTP than those exposed to convenience proposition.; T2: Creators exposed to convenience proposition will show higher purchase intent and WTP than those exposed to professional-grade proposition.. Decision rule: If the proportion of creators who indicate "Would buy" for the professional-grade proposition is at least 55% and their WTP is at least €200, proceed to develop a differentiated home-studio proposition. If the convenience proposition meets the same thresholds, also proceed. If neither meets thresholds, keep the current professional range.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Develop a differentiated home-studio proposition that emphasizes professional-grade sound quality and credibility, while also highlighting the convenience of Neumann’s integrated solutions. Recommendation: Develop a differentiated home-studio proposition that emphasizes professional-grade sound quality and credibility, while also highlighting the convenience of Neumann’s integrated solutions. Use the existing Home Studio Academy content to reinforce the value proposition and test purchase intent with a targeted survey. Target customer: Home-studio creators who produce content for personal or small-scale professional use, currently using lower-cost gear that lacks professional sound quality.. Value proposition: A premium, professional-grade microphone and monitor system that delivers consistent, high-quality recordings, backed by Neumann’s reputation for sound excellence and integrated workflow convenience.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Differentiated Consumer Proposition" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios.. Sample: 500 UK adults recruited via an online panel, split equally between outdoor/recreation and work/construction segments.. Measure: Willingness-to-pay (WTP) for a differentiated earplug product (stylish vs safety-focused) and intent to purchase.. Predictions: T1: Higher WTP and purchase intent for the styled earplug in the outdoor/recreation segment.; T2: Higher WTP and purchase intent for the safety-focused earplug in the work/construction segment.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the styled earplug exceeds the average WTP for the safety-focused earplug by at least 20% in the outdoor segment, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition. If the safety-focused earplug exceeds the styled earplug by at least 20% in the work segment, prioritize a safety-focused proposition. If neither segment meets the 20% threshold, do not expand.. Cost: 12000 euros, 8 weeks.

Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Households will purchase a differentiated consumer proposition because they view the tractor as a versatile tool for small-scale tasks, and Deere can capture value by selling a branded, differentiated unit at a premium price. Who benefits: Individual homeowners and small garden owners who need a tool for mowing, weeding, and light cleanup.. Why behaviour changes: Growing household garden size and interest in DIY in the 1960s make a dedicated lawn tractor attractive; the tractor's versatility and Deere's brand signal quality justify a premium purchase.. How value is captured: Deere sells a branded, differentiated unit through independent dealers at a higher price point than generic tractors, earning margin on the product.. Assumptions: Households in 1962 have sufficient disposable income to buy a dedicated lawn tractor.; Deere's engineering reputation translates into consumer trust.; Independent dealers can effectively promote and sell a differentiated product.. Predictions: In a test offering a branded lawn tractor at a 20% premium over a generic equivalent, purchase intent among target homeowners will be at least 15% higher than for a generic tractor.; Sales conversion rate will be at least 5% among households shown the branded unit..

T2: Households will purchase a differentiated consumer proposition because they need a tool for a specific, recurring task (e.g., mowing) and prefer a dedicated unit over a versatile tractor, leading Deere to capture value through a specialized line of lawn tractors. Who benefits: Individual homeowners who need a dedicated mower for regular, small-scale tasks.. Why behaviour changes: The rise of suburban home ownership and the increasing importance of regular lawn care create a demand for a specialized tool; a dedicated mower is perceived as more efficient and reliable than a versatile tractor.. How value is captured: Deere sells a specialized lawn mower at a premium price through independent dealers, earning margin on a dedicated product line.. Recruit via panel to ensure demographic overlap with 1962 U.S. market.. Measure: Purchase intent: binary choice “Would you buy this lawn tractor?” with a “Yes” rate. Secondary measure: stated primary reason (convenience vs versatility vs cost savings).. Predictions: T1: Homeowners will show higher “Yes” rate than small‑farm owners, and convenience will be the top reason.; T2: Small‑farm owners will show higher “Yes” rate than homeowners, and versatility will be the top reason.. Decision rule: If homeowners’ “Yes” rate exceeds small‑farm owners’ “Yes” rate by at least 10 percentage points, proceed with differentiated homeowner proposition. If small‑farm owners’ “Yes” rate exceeds homeowners’ “Yes” rate by at least 10 percentage points, proceed with differentiated small‑farm proposition. If both rates are equal or difference is ≤ 10 percentage points, no. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Who benefits: Consumers seeking comfortable, discreet protection for outdoor recreation and leisure.. Who benefits: Professional and industrial workers, medical staff, and high-risk enthusiasts who need compliance with safety standards.. Why behaviour changes: If hearing protection is framed as mandatory for a specific use case, consumers will purchase it to meet regulatory or job requirements, even if it is less comfortable or stylish.. How value is captured: Hellberg can sell premium, certified products through B2B channels and safety suppliers, capturing higher margins and volume sales.. Test "Leisure vs Safety Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from two groups: Leisure Group (n=200) and Safety Group (n=200). Both groups see a product description of a hearing protection device for a specific use case (e.g., hiking, hunting, medical). Leisure group sees a lifestyle framing: "Comfortable, stylish earplugs for your outdoor adventures." Safety group sees a safety framing: "Certified hearing protection required for this activity." Both groups are offered a pre-order at a fixed price (e.g., €50).. Sample: 2,000 adult consumers (1,000 per group) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would you pre-order this product?") and willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7-point scale.. Predictions: T1: Leisure group will show higher purchase intent and WTP than Safety group, indicating demand for a lifestyle proposition.; T2: Safety group will show higher purchase intent and WTP than Leisure group, indicating demand for a safety requirement framing.. Decision rule: If Leisure group purchase intent exceeds Safety group purchase intent by at least 10 percentage points (e.g., 55% vs 45%), proceed to develop a differentiated leisure proposition. If Safety group purchase intent exceeds Leisure group by at least 10 percentage points, develop a safety-focused proposition. If the difference is below 10 points, no expansion is recommended.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting outdoor and leisure activities, framed as a lifestyle accessory that emphasizes comfort and style. Begin with a small-scale online pre-order test to validate purchase intent and willingness to pay before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated result SYN-A shows that styled protectors did not increase wear frequency compared to plain ones, which contradicts T1's assumption that consumers will adopt a differentiated product if it is styled. Therefore T1 is not supported by evidence. New claim: Consumers will adopt differentiated hearing protection if it is marketed as a safety requirement for specific high-risk activities, because they view it as a legal or professional necessity rather than a lifestyle accessory.. Evidence: SYN-A.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting outdoor and leisure activities, framed as a lifestyle accessory that emphasizes comfort and style. Begin with a small-scale online pre-order test to validate purchase intent and willingness to pay before scaling. Target customer: Adult consumers who engage in outdoor and leisure activities (hiking, cycling, hunting, concerts, school activities) and value comfort and aesthetics in hearing protection.. Value proposition: Stylish, comfortable hearing protection designed for specific leisure activities, offering peace of mind and enhanced enjoyment of outdoor experiences.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Leisure vs Safety Messaging Test (2,000 participants, 10-week timeline, €18,000 budget) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay under lifestyle versus safety framing.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for hearing protection and the actual willingness to pay for a differentiated product are uncertain. Evidence shows styled protectors do not increase wear frequency (SYN-A), which weakens T1's assumption.. Would change if: If the test shows the Safety group (high-risk framing) achieving purchase intent at least 10 percentage points higher than the Leisure group, we would shift focus to a safety requirement proposition.; If the test shows no significant difference in purchase intent between the two framing groups, we would reconsider expansion or explore other alternatives.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Home-Studio Creator Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with choice-based conjoint design. Participants are recruited from home-studio creators (self-identified) and shown two product concepts: (1) Affordable Professional Line (lower price, similar performance, brand reputation) and (2) Premium Professional Line (higher price, exclusive features, strong brand reputation). They indicate which concept they would purchase and the maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 300 participants: 150 self-identified home-studio creators (recruited via social media and forums), 150 control participants (non-creators).. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and maximum willingness-to-pay (EUR).. Predictions: T1: At least 60% of creators will choose the Affordable Professional Line and indicate willingness to pay up to 20% less than the Premium Line.; T2: At least 60% of creators will choose the Premium Professional Line and indicate willingness to pay a premium of at least 20% over the Affordable Line.. Decision rule: If the Affordable Line's purchase intent ≥ 60% and its maximum price ≤ 20% of the Premium Line's price, recommend developing an affordable differentiated proposition. If the Premium Line's purchase intent ≥ 60% and its price is at least 20% above the Affordable Line, recommend a premium differentiated proposition. If neither condition is met, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Develop a differentiated affordable home-studio proposition (e.g., lower-cost, specialized features) for individual creators, while retaining the premium professional line. How value is captured: Tanita can sell a lower‑priced consumer line through retail channels, capturing value through higher volume sales and lower per‑unit cost.. Assumptions: Consumers prioritize ease of use over detailed accuracy.; A one‑button measurement reduces perceived complexity.; Retail distribution can reach target consumers effectively.. T1: Households will adopt a lawn tractor if it is marketed as a convenient, single-use tool for small gardens, because the task is too small for a farm tractor and too small for a garden tool, so a differentiated consumer proposition captures a new segment. Who benefits: Households with small gardens who need a quick, one-time chore. Why behaviour changes: They currently use a shovel or push mower for small jobs; a dedicated lawn tractor removes the need to switch tools and reduces chores.. How value is captured: Deere sells a differentiated model through independent dealers at a premium price, capturing margin on a new consumer segment.. Assumptions: Households in 1962 have small gardens and need a quick chore solution; Independent dealers can reach these households; Marketing can differentiate the product from existing garden tools. Predictions: Surveyed households will indicate willingness to purchase a dedicated lawn tractor for small gardens; Sales of a differentiated model will be higher in regions with small garden ownership than in large farm regions.

T2: Households will adopt a lawn tractor if it is marketed as a multi-use tool for small gardens and light outdoor work, because they need one device that can handle mowing, weeding, and light cleanup, so a differentiated proposition captures a broader functional need. Who benefits: Households with small gardens and light outdoor work that currently require multiple tools. Why behaviour changes: They currently use a shovel, push mower, and hand tools for small jobs; a single, versatile lawn tractor reduces tool switching and chores.. How value is captured: Deere sells a differentiated model through independent dealers at a premium price, capturing margin on a multi-functional product.. Assumptions: Households in 1962 have small gardens and need a versatile tool; Marketing can emphasize multi-use capabilities; Independent dealers can stock and promote a versatile lawn tractor. Predictions: Surveyed households will indicate willingness to purchase a versatile lawn tractor for multiple tasks; Sales of a differentiated model will be higher in regions with small garden ownership and light outdoor work than in large farm regions.

Test "Consumer Proposition Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 400 U.S. households recruited via an online panel, balanced across regions with small garden ownership (east coast) and large farm regions (Midwest).. Measure: 1) WTP for a differentiated lawn tractor marketed as a single-use tool (T1) vs a versatile tool (T2). 2) Intent to purchase (binary: "Would buy" vs "Would not buy").. Predictions: T1: WTP for the single-use proposition will be higher than for the versatile proposition in small garden regions.; T2: WTP for the versatile proposition will be higher than for the single-use proposition in small garden regions.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the single-use proposition in small garden regions exceeds the average WTP for the versatile proposition by at least 10% (e.g., €200 vs €180), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the opposite difference holds, pursue a versatile proposition. If the difference is below 10%, do not commit to a differentiated proposition and consider other alternatives.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not commit to a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows a prototype was built in 1959 and sales rose 76% in 1960-1979, but it does not show household demand for a single-use lawn tractor. Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Preference Test to measure willingness-to-pay and purchase intent before investing. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not commit to a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows a prototype was built in 1959 and sales rose 76% in 1960-1979, but it does not show household demand for a single-use lawn tractor. Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Preference Test to measure willingness-to-pay and purchase intent before investing. Target customer: Households with small gardens who need a quick, one-time chore solution. Value proposition: A differentiated lawn tractor marketed as a convenient, single-use tool for small gardens, sold through independent dealers at a premium price.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Execute the Consumer Proposition Preference Test (400 households, 6 weeks, €18,000) to compare willingness-to-pay for single-use vs versatile propositions.. Uncertainty: Whether households in 1962 actually need a dedicated lawn tractor for small gardens and are willing to pay a premium for it.. Would change if: If the test shows the versatile proposition (T2) has higher willingness-to-pay in small garden regions, we would shift to a multi-functional proposition.; If the test shows no significant difference or lower willingness-to-pay for the single-use proposition, we would reconsider the investment or pursue other alternatives.. Why behaviour changes: Shifting perception from mandatory safety gear to optional, stylish accessory reduces perceived barrier to purchase and increases willingness to pay for design and comfort.. How value is captured: Hellberg can price higher for differentiated designs, sell through retail and online channels, and capture margin on premium products.. Assumptions: Consumers currently view hearing protection as utilitarian rather than fashion.; A differentiated design can be produced at a cost that allows premium pricing.; Retail and online channels can reach target consumers effectively.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate higher intent to purchase a differentiated product compared to a standard safety product.; Purchase intent will correlate with perceived style and comfort rather than safety certification alone..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive hearing protection as a medical necessity, particularly for occupational and high-risk activities, because they trust safety certifications and regulatory compliance. Who benefits: Occupational safety managers and workers who need certified protection; Hellberg Safety gains credibility and can meet regulatory requirements.. Why behaviour changes: Regulatory demand and trust in certified standards create a perceived need for compliant protection, prompting purchases even without lifestyle appeal.. How value is captured: Hellberg can market products as compliant, sell through safety distributors, and capture margin on certified, high-risk products.. Assumptions: Regulatory requirements for hearing protection are clear and enforceable.; Consumers trust safety certifications over design alone.; Occupational buyers are willing to pay for certified protection.. Predictions: Surveyed occupational buyers will indicate higher purchase intent for certified products compared to unbranded alternatives.; Purchase decisions will be driven by certification status rather than style or comfort..

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Lifestyle vs. Medical Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated product offers. Sample: 500 respondents: 250 self-identified outdoor/recreational consumers and 250 occupational safety professionals. Measure: Purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay (EUR) for a differentiated product described with either lifestyle or medical messaging. Predictions: T1: Lifestyle messaging will achieve higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than medical messaging.; T2: Medical messaging will achieve higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than lifestyle messaging.. Decision rule: If lifestyle messaging achieves ≥15 points higher purchase intent than medical messaging, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting outdoor/recreational use. If medical messaging achieves ≥15 points higher purchase intent, pursue a differentiated proposition targeting occupational use. If both messaging types achieve similar intent, no further action is recommended.. Cost: 8000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting outdoor/recreational use, leveraging Hellberg’s design expertise and existing retail presence. Begin with a small pilot test to validate consumer willingness to pay for a lifestyle‑focused product. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated result SYN-B concerns wear comfort and does not address consumer perception of hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory or medical necessity. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-B.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting outdoor/recreational use, leveraging Hellberg’s design expertise and existing retail presence. Begin with a small pilot test to validate consumer willingness to pay for a lifestyle‑focused product. Target customer: Outdoor/recreational consumers (hiking, cycling, music enthusiasts) who currently use standard hearing protection but seek comfort and style.. Value proposition: A differentiated hearing protection product that combines advanced comfort, stylish design, and EN 352 certification, positioned as an optional accessory for enhanced enjoyment of activities.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (500 respondents, 10 weeks, €8,000) to compare lifestyle vs. medical messaging. Use the decision rule: if lifestyle messaging achieves ≥5 points higher purchase intent, proceed to develop the pilot;. Uncertainty: Consumer willingness to pay for a differentiated proposition is unknown; the test will resolve this. Additionally, the extent to which consumers perceive hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory versus a medical necessity is uncertain.. Would change if: If the pilot shows lifestyle messaging achieving ≥5 points lower purchase intent than medical messaging, we would reconsider the proposition and focus on occupational use.; If new evidence shows strong regulatory demand for hearing protection in occupational settings, we would shift focus to a medical necessity proposition.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Households will adopt a lawn tractor if it is marketed as a convenient, single-use tool for small gardens, because the task is too small for a farm tractor and too small for a hand tool, so a differentiated consumer proposition captures a new segment. Who benefits: Households with small gardens who need a quick, one-time chore. Why behaviour changes: They currently use hand tools or small hand tractors for garden chores, but a dedicated lawn tractor removes the need to switch tools and reduces chores to a single task. How value is captured: Deere sells a differentiated lawn tractor at a premium price through independent dealers, capturing margin on a new consumer segment. Assumptions: Households in 1962 have small gardens and need a quick chore; Marketing can differentiate the product from farm tractors; Independent dealers can reach these households. Predictions: Households will purchase a lawn tractor for a specific garden chore rather than a general farm tractor; Sales will be concentrated in regions with small garden ownership; Deere will achieve higher per-unit margin than its farm tractors.

T2: Households will adopt a lawn tractor if it is marketed as a versatile tool for multiple small garden tasks, because they need one machine that can mow, rake, and clear leaves, so a differentiated proposition captures a broader use case. Who benefits: Households with small gardens who need multiple tasks. Why behaviour changes: They currently use separate tools for mowing, raking, and leaf removal, so a single, versatile lawn tractor reduces the number of tools they need and simplifies chores. How value is captured: Deere sells a differentiated lawn tractor with multiple attachments at a premium price through independent dealers, capturing margin on a versatile product. Assumptions: Households in 1962 have small gardens and need multiple tasks; Marketing can highlight the versatility of the lawn tractor; Independent dealers can stock and promote multiple attachments. Predictions: Households will purchase a lawn tractor for multiple garden tasks rather than a single task; Sales will be concentrated in regions with larger small gardens; Deere will achieve higher per-unit margin than its farm tractors.

Test "Consumer Preference Test for Lawn Tractor Use Case" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Sample: 500 U.S. households recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and garden size (small vs. large).. Measure: 1) Choice: prefer a single-use lawn tractor for a specific garden chore (T1) or a versatile lawn tractor for multiple tasks (T2). 2) Willingness to pay: maximum price they would pay for each option. 3) Purchase intent: would buy the product if price was met.. Predictions: T1: Households will choose the single-use lawn tractor for a specific chore and show higher willingness to pay for that option, indicating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition focused on convenience.; T2: Households will choose the versatile lawn tractor for multiple tasks and show higher willingness to pay for that option, indicating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition focused on versatility.. Decision rule: If the single-use lawn tractor receives at least 55% of choices and at least 55% of respondents indicate willingness to pay at least $1,500, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case. If the versatile lawn tractor receives at least 55% of choices and at least 55% of respondents indicate willingness to pay at least $1,500, develop a differentiated consumer proposition for multiple tasks. If neither meets the thresholds, do not invest.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows a prototype was built in 1959 and sales rose 76% in 1960-1979, but it does not show households will purchase a single-use lawn tractor or that it meets a specific use case. Run the proposed consumer preference test to measure demand for a single-use lawn tractor before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer demand for a single-use lawn tractor. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows a prototype was built in 1959 and sales rose 76% in 1960-1979, but it does not show households will purchase a single-use lawn tractor or that it meets a specific use case. Run the proposed consumer preference test to measure demand for a single-use lawn tractor before committing resources. Target customer: Households with small gardens who need a quick, one-time chore. Value proposition: A differentiated lawn tractor marketed as a convenient, single-use tool for small garden chores, sold through independent dealers at a premium price.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the Consumer Preference Test (500 households, 10 weeks, €15,000) to measure choice and willingness to pay for a single-use lawn tractor versus a versatile lawn tractor.. Uncertainty: Demand for a single-use lawn tractor is unknown; the test will resolve this. Also uncertain is whether households will pay a premium price and whether independent dealers can effectively reach these households.. Would change if: If the test shows the versatile lawn tractor receives at least 55% of choices and willingness to pay meets the threshold, we would shift to a differentiated proposition for multiple tasks.; If the test shows neither option meets the thresholds, we would maintain the current business model with no expansion.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Home-studio creators will adopt Neumann products if they perceive the equipment as a professional-grade tool that delivers high-quality sound, because they value performance over cost and are willing to invest in tools they trust for their work. Who benefits: Home-studio creators who produce music, podcasting, or video content and need reliable studio equipment.. Why behaviour changes: When creators see Neumann products recommended by peers or reviewed as professional-grade, they shift from generic consumer gear to professional-grade tools because they associate quality with credibility and better results.. How value is captured: Neumann can charge premium prices for its professional-grade products and capture recurring revenue through accessories, upgrades, and maintenance services, leveraging its reputation for audio quality.. Assumptions: Creators are aware of Neumann's professional reputation and can distinguish it from consumer brands.; Quality perception translates into purchase intent and actual purchase behavior.; The market size for individual creators is large enough to justify a differentiated proposition.. Predictions: Creators will show higher purchase intent when presented with professional-grade positioning compared to a generic positioning.; Sales of professional-grade Neumann products will increase in regions where creators are concentrated.; Willingness to pay for premium features will be higher among creators than for general consumers..

T2: Home-studio creators will adopt Neumann products if they perceive the equipment as a status symbol or brand association, because they seek to signal professionalism and credibility to their audience, even if the price is higher. Who benefits: Home-studio creators who want to project expertise and professionalism to their audience, such as musicians, podcasters, and content creators.. Why behaviour changes: When creators view Neumann as a premium brand associated with professionalism, they are motivated to purchase it to enhance their image and gain respect from peers and followers, leading to higher willingness to pay.. How value is captured: Neumann can command premium pricing and capture value through brand licensing, limited-edition collaborations, and premium accessories that reinforce the professional image.. Assumptions: Creators are aware of and value brand prestige in the audio industry.; Social proof and peer influence drive purchase decisions for professional-grade equipment.; The market for individual creators is large enough to support a premium positioning.. Predictions: Creators will show higher purchase intent when presented with brand positioning that emphasizes professionalism and prestige.; Sales of premium-priced Neumann products will be concentrated in regions where creators have a strong social presence.; Willingness to pay for brand-related features will be higher among creators than for general consumers..

Test "Home-Studio Creator Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 500 self-identified home-studio creators (music producers, podcasters, content creators) from the US and Germany, recruited via creator forums and social media.. Yes/No). 2) WTP: maximum price they would pay for a professional-grade Neumann product (EUR). 3) Brand perception: Likert scale for how much they associate Neumann with professionalism and prestige.. Predictions: T1: Creators shown professional-grade positioning will have higher purchase intent and WTP than those shown brand positioning.; T2: Creators shown brand positioning will have higher purchase intent and WTP than those shown professional-grade positioning.. events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available by late 2002 to justify ACR Electronics investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology.. Constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive landscape for a consumer product.; Must consider ACR’s existing B2B products (shipping, aircraft, military, marine) and its current reach to individual buyers.; Must assess regulatory and market feasibility of a consumer product using satellite distress beacons.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual users (e.g., marine recreational users, outdoor enthusiasts) with a dedicated product line and marketing.; 2) Expand the existing B2B product line into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add a consumer‑focused version of the beacon for marine recreational users).; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B customers and existing product portfolio.; 4) License the 406 MHz technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer products, capturing value through royalties rather than direct consumer sales..

T1: Individual buyers will purchase a consumer-grade 406 MHz satellite distress beacon primarily for marine recreational activities because they perceive it as a safety necessity for extended trips and as a way to communicate with search and rescue authorities. Who benefits: Marine recreational users (boaters, campers, hikers) who need reliable emergency communication in remote areas.. Why behaviour changes: They currently rely on cell phones, radios, or GPS devices that may not work in remote areas; a dedicated beacon provides a guaranteed distress signal that can be detected by search and rescue satellites.. How value is captured: ACR would sell the beacon directly to consumers through outdoor retailers or online channels, charging a premium price based on the device’s reliability and the perceived safety benefit.. Assumptions: Marine recreational participation in the U.S. is large enough to generate demand for a consumer product.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a device that guarantees rescue in life-threatening situations.; The 406 MHz technology is technically feasible and meets regulatory requirements for consumer use.. Predictions: In a survey of marine recreational users, at least 30% would indicate they would purchase a consumer-grade PLB for their next trip.; Willingness to pay for a consumer-grade PLB will be at least $150, with higher willingness among users who frequently travel in remote areas..

T2: Individual buyers will purchase a consumer-grade 406 MHz satellite distress beacon primarily for emergency preparedness and disaster response, because they are increasingly concerned about natural disasters and need a reliable way to signal for help. Who benefits: Homeowners, renters, and small property owners in disaster-prone areas who want to protect themselves and their families.. case.question: It is 1993. Should Tanita develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser for clinics and health clubs? What evidence would justify that investment?

Based on medical evidence linking excess body fat to heart disease, diabetes and certain cancers, Tanita introduced the world’s first integrated body composition analyzer/scale to the professional markets in 1992.
Tanita is a world leader in precision electronic scales. With almost 50% of its domestic market share, the name Tanita is a household name in Japan.
In Japan, every household has a bathroom scale (health meter), and most nowadays keep track of your body composition.

A body fat measuring apparatus for measuring body fat in a patient's body comprises apparatus for simultaneously measuring an impedance between the patient's feet, and for measuring the patient's height and the patient's weight

the impedance value of a body to be measured vary according to the date, time and differences of body condition before measurement. These various are too large to use the above-described inference formula accurately and amount of body fat calculated by the formula is likely to be inaccurate.
In 104 men and 101 women (16-78 years and BMI 16-41 kg/m2) the mean bias in body-fat mass measured using the Tanita body-fat analyser was 0.8 (2SD 7.9) kg relative to a four-compartment model.

This method is safe, noninvasive, provides rapid measurements, requires little operator skill and subject cooperation, and is portable. Further validation of this method is recommended in subjects with abnormal body composition.
The Tanita TBF-310 foot-to-foot BIA body composition analyser with the manufacturer's prediction equations is not recommended for application to individual children who are overweight and obese

events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in 1993 to justify Tanita investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its stand‑on bioelectrical impedance body‑fat analyser, by evaluating demand, market fit, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.. Constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; no internal company data.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Evidence must address consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning; no financial data available.; Any recommendation must be based on observable market behavior, not speculation about future outcomes.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home users for a specific use case (e.g., weight management, fitness tracking).; 2) Expand the existing B2B offering by adding new features or marketing channels to clinics and health clubs without a consumer focus.; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B market (clinics and health clubs).; 4) License the technology to third‑party manufacturers to create consumer devices, capturing value through royalties rather than direct sales..

T1: Consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if they perceive it as a health necessity, and are willing to pay a premium for accurate, non-invasive body-fat measurement. Who benefits: Health-conscious consumers seeking precise body-fat information for weight management.. Why behaviour changes: Increased awareness of health risks (heart disease, diabetes) and media promotion of body-fat tracking create demand for accurate home measurement.. How value is captured: Tanita can charge a premium price for a differentiated consumer device, leveraging its existing B2B reputation for precision.. Assumptions: Consumers trust medical evidence linking excess body fat to health risks.; Media and health campaigns effectively reach target consumers in 1993.; Consumers are willing to pay more for a device they perceive as a health tool.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% more for a home body-fat analyser compared to a standard bathroom scale.; Purchase intent will be higher among individuals with a body mass index (BMI) above 25 than among those with BMI below 25..

T2: Consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if it offers a convenient, one‑button measurement without requiring separate foot contact, reducing user effort and increasing compliance. Who benefits: Time‑constrained consumers who prefer quick, no‑foot‑contact health checks.. Why behaviour changes: Effort reduction and convenience make the device more attractive than traditional scales that require separate foot placement.. How value is captured: Tanita can market a simplified version of its existing analyser, leveraging the same precision to capture a new consumer segment at a modest price premium.. Assumptions: Consumers prioritize ease of use over the accuracy of foot-to-foot versus four-compartment measurements.; A one‑button interface is feasible with existing technology and does not compromise accuracy.; Marketing can effectively communicate the convenience benefit to potential buyers.. Predictions: Consumers will report higher purchase intent for a one‑button device compared to a standard stand‑on scale.; Willingness to pay for the simplified device will be at least 15% lower than for a standard stand‑on scale, but still above a basic bathroom scale..

T1 supports, from tanita-dic-origin (company_assertion): "Based on medical evidence linking excess body fat to heart disease, diabetes and certain cancers". Does not show: It does not show consumer demand or willingness to pay for a home device; it only establishes the medical basis for body-fat measurement..

T2 supports, from tanita-pm-jebb (independent_study): "In 104 men and 101 women (16-78 years and BMI 16-41 kg/m2) the mean bias in body-fat mass measured using the Tanita body-fat analyser was 0.8 (2SD 7.9) kg relative to a four-compartment model.". Does not show: It does not show that a one-button device would be more accurate or that consumers would prefer it; it only compares the existing four-compartment model..

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Foot-to-Foot vs One-Button Measurement" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to view either a standard four-compartment body-fat analyser description (T1) or a one-button foot-to-foot device description (T2). They are then asked to indicate willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent on a 7-point scale.. Sample: 300 adults aged 18-65, recruited via an online panel, balanced for BMI (BMI <25 and BMI ≥25).. Measure: Average WTP (in euros) and purchase intent (on a 7-point scale) for each condition.. Predictions: T1: Higher average WTP and purchase intent for the four-compartment device than for the one-button device.; T2: Higher average WTP and purchase intent for the one-button device than for the four-compartment device.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the four-compartment device exceeds the average WTP for the one-button device by at least 15% (e.g., €15), proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting health-conscious users. If the one-button device's WTP exceeds the four-compartment device's WTP by at least 15%, develop a simplified, one-button consumer version. If neither difference meets the 15% threshold, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public sources show Tanita already sells a stand-on body-fat analyser to clinics and health clubs, and there is no evidence of consumer demand or willingness to pay for a home device. The 12‑week test budget and 20,000€ limit would be better spent validating a specific use case (e.g., weight management) rather than launching a broad consumer line. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing efficiency and does not address consumer demand, willingness to pay, or the specific use case of a home body-fat analyser. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public sources show Tanita already sells a stand-on body-fat analyser to clinics and health clubs, and there is no evidence of consumer demand or willingness to pay for a home device. The 12‑week test budget and 20,000€ limit would be better spent validating a specific use case (e.g., weight management) rather than launching a broad consumer line. Target customer: Health‑conscious consumers aged 18‑65 who seek precise body‑fat information for weight management, particularly those with a body mass index (BMI) above 25.. Value proposition: A differentiated home body‑fat analyser that leverages Tanita’s existing B2B reputation for precision, offering accurate, non‑invasive measurements at a premium price.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (300 adults, 6 weeks, €18,000) to compare willingness to pay and purchase intent for a standard four‑compartment device versus a simplified one‑button foot‑to‑foot device.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market, willingness to pay a premium, and the feasibility of a simplified one‑button interface remain uncertain. Public sources do not provide financial data or direct evidence of consumer demand.. Would change if: If the test shows the one‑button device achieving a willingness to pay at least 15% higher than the four‑compartment device, we would reconsider developing a simplified consumer version.; If new public sources from 1993 reveal strong consumer demand or price sensitivity for home body‑fat analysers, we would reassess the investment case.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1: Homeowners will adopt garden tractors because they view them as a convenient, single‑tool solution for small‑scale landscaping and yard work, reducing the need for multiple tools and labor. Who benefits: Individual homeowners who need to clear grass, rake leaves, or move mulch without hiring help.. Why behaviour changes: The growing household garden size and the perception of tractors as inexpensive and easy to maintain make them an attractive, one‑time purchase rather than a series of tools.. How value is captured: Deere can capture value by selling a differentiated consumer model at a premium price, leveraging its tractor engineering to offer durability and performance that justify higher cost.. Assumptions: Homeowners in 1962 have sufficient disposable income to purchase a garden tractor.; The market for small‑scale landscaping is large enough to support a consumer line.; Deere can produce a consumer‑grade tractor that meets homeowner expectations for ease of use and durability.. Predictions: A survey of homeowners would show higher intent to buy a garden tractor than a comparable farm tractor.; Sales of a consumer‑focused model would be higher in regions with larger household gardens.; Customers would cite convenience and cost savings as primary purchase reasons..

T2: Homeowners will adopt garden tractors because they view them as a status symbol and status signal, indicating modernity and capability, especially among middle‑class households. Who benefits: Middle‑class homeowners who want to demonstrate financial stability and modern living standards.. Why behaviour changes: The 1960s consumer culture emphasizes ownership of modern, convenient goods; a garden tractor becomes a visible marker of success and ability to manage a garden.. How value is captured: Deere can capture value by positioning a consumer model as a premium, status‑friendly product, justifying higher price through brand prestige and design.. Assumptions: Middle‑class households in 1962 value visible status and modernity.; A garden tractor can be marketed as a status item rather than a utilitarian tool.; Deere can design and price a model that appeals to status‑conscious buyers.. Predictions: A survey of homeowners would rank garden tractors higher for status than for practical utility.; Sales would be concentrated in regions where middle‑class households are more visible.; Customers would cite status and prestige as primary purchase reasons..

Test "Consumer Proposition Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios and stated reasons.. Otherwise, do not invest.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Who benefits: Hellberg Safety gains higher margins and brand equity by positioning products as fashion or lifestyle items.. Who benefits: Hellberg Safety gains market share in high‑risk segments and can command premium prices for specialized protection.. Why behaviour changes: Regulatory or safety requirements for a particular use case create a clear need for effective protection, prompting consumers to purchase specialized products rather than generic safety gear.. Test "Consumer Positioning Test: Lifestyle vs High‑Risk Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated product offers. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Group A sees a lifestyle‑focused description emphasizing fashion, comfort, and multiple use cases (e.g., concerts, outdoor recreation). Group B sees a high‑risk‑focused description emphasizing safety regulations, industrial use, and specialized protection (e.g., construction, mining). Both groups are presented with a price point and a willingness‑to‑pay survey. The test measures the difference in average willingness to pay (EUR) between the two groups.. Sample: 500 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced between gender and age to reflect general consumer base.. Measure: Average willingness to pay (EUR) for the product described in each group.. Predictions: T1: Group A will show a higher average willingness to pay than Group B.; T2: Group B will show a higher average willingness to pay than Group A.. Decision rule: If the difference in average willingness to pay between Group A and Group B exceeds €5 (a threshold derived from the 10% price elasticity of safety products), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting the respective use case. If the difference is below €5, no further investment is justified.. Cost: 8000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory, targeting specific use cases such as outdoor recreation, concerts, and school activities. Begin with a limited launch of a design-led product and retail presence to test consumer willingness to pay and adoption. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory, targeting specific use cases such as outdoor recreation, concerts, and school activities. Begin with a limited launch of a design-led product and retail presence to test consumer willingness to pay and adoption. Target customer: Adult consumers who engage in activities where hearing protection is currently optional or not required, such as outdoor enthusiasts, concert-goers, and school children.. Value proposition: A lifestyle-oriented hearing protection product that combines comfort, style, and functionality, offering multiple use cases and premium pricing to capture higher margins and brand equity.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer Positioning Test (500 participants, 6 weeks, €8,000) to measure willingness to pay for lifestyle versus high‑risk messaging. Use the €5 price‑elasticity threshold to decide whether to proceed with development.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for lifestyle hearing protection and the actual willingness to pay premium prices are uncertain. Evidence from the test will resolve whether T1 is supported or requires revision.. Would change if: If the test shows no significant difference in willingness to pay between lifestyle and high‑risk messaging (difference < €5), the investment case weakens and the recommendation would shift toward maintaining the current business model.; If additional evidence shows strong consumer demand for specialized protection in high‑risk use cases, the recommendation would shift toward developing a differentiated high‑risk proposition.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available by late 2002 to justify ACR Electronics investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology.. Constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive landscape for a consumer product.; Must consider ACR’s existing B2B products (shipping, aircraft, military, marine) and its current reach to individual buyers.; Must assess regulatory and market feasibility of a consumer product using satellite distress beacons.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual users (e.g., marine recreational users, outdoor enthusiasts) with a dedicated product line and marketing.; 2) Expand the existing B2B product line into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add a consumer‑focused version of the beacon for marine recreational users).; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B customers and existing product portfolio.; 4) License the 406 MHz technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer products, capturing value through royalties rather than direct consumer sales..
